speechtext:
1.	Referring to the Prime Minister's statement at page 671 of the Hansard of December 5,

Questions
1940, after the governor general ceased to be, on July 1, 1927, "the channel of communication between the government of Canada and the government of the United Kingdom", how long was the government of Canada without "a channel of communication" between itself and the government of the United Kingdom?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

speechtext:
1.	At no time.
2.	Before 1925, the Governor General reported to the Secretary of State for the Colonies. From July, 1925, to July 1, 1927, His Excellency reported to the Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs.
3.	In 1928.
4.	The United Kingdom High Commissioner in Ottawa is one channel of communication between the government of the United Kingdom and the government of Canada.
5.	The United Kingdom High Commissioner in Ottawa reports to the Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs.
6.	No.
7.	There are continual changes in the relations between the government of Canada and the government of the United Kingdom, as is the case in the relations between the government of Canada and any other government.
8.	No.
9.	No.
10.	Immigration questions which concern both governments have, from time to time,, been discussed through the various channels of communication between the governments of the United Kingdom and of Canada.
11.	It is for the government of the United Kingdom to define the duties of the United Kingdom High Commissioner in Canada; he reports to the Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs. The duties of the Canadian High Commissioner in the United Kingdom are defined as follows by section 3 of the acts of parliament of Canada, 2 George VI, chapter 30:
(3) The High Commissioner for Canada in the United Kingdom shall,-(a) act as representative and resident agent of Canada in the United Kingdom, and, in that capacity, execute such powers and perform such duties as are, from time to time, conferred upon and assigned to him by the governor in council; (b) carry out such instructions as he, from time to time, receives from the Secretary of State for External Affairs respecting the general interests of Canada in the United Kingdom; (c) subject to the provisions of the preceding paragraphs, supervise the official activities of the various agencies of the Canadian government in the United Kingdom.

Certified to be a true copy of a minute of a meeting of the committee of the privy council, approved by His Excellency the Governor General on the 22nd March, 1943.
The committee of the privy council have had before them a report, dated 19th March, 1943, from the Minister of Labour, representing that the department is obligated to locate the whereabouts of certain individuals to whom the divisional registrars have been unable to deliver first call-up notices for military service;

speechtext: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee of ways and means.

subtopic: OPPORTUNITY FOR DISCUSSION OF CANADA'S WAR POSITION-STATEMENT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the house resolves itself into committee of ways and means, I wish to speak very briefly on something which I could not have discussed on the orders of the day, because I wanted to say more than would be proper then.
The house has been in session for nine weeks. Within a short time we shall be returning to our constituencies. So far there has been no opportunity for a clear statement in this house of the war position. Instead of making statements in the budget debate and in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the ministers of defence and other departments have been waiting for the war appropriation bill1 to come down; and since the house has been delayed in reaching that order of business it seems to me that before the house adjourns for the Easter recess some opportunity should be given us to understand what the situation really is. We realize that there are certain matters that cannot well be disclosed publicly in this chamber-not because the people of Canada, should not be made aware of everything that is being done or left undone, but because there are certain matters that might give aid and comfort to the enemy or information which would enable him to go forward with plans to meet what we propose to do. But the House of Commons is entitled to a clear statement at the earliest possible day, certainly before the Easter recess. We as private members should impress upon the government that even in war time this parliament is responsible to the people, and that

the government, or the cabinet, is not the master but the creature of this House of Commons and ought at all times to be subject to its will.
I have been alarmed1 during the last four or five years at the extent to which parliament has in some respects taken on the form of the totalitarian states in that from time to time we have become merely a sounding board for the making of statements and pronouncements, when we were favoured with such. At this point I wish to refer to the making of statements of policy, involving important decisions of which this house should be apprised and which it should if it deems fit, approve, on the orders of the day thus preventing any possibility of discussion of those important statements in this chamber. The house is losing the control of the executive arm of the government which ought properly to be ours. It is time that hon. members took the opportunity to remind the government that the sovereign governing power in this country after all is parliament, not the cabinet or the government of the day. The time has surely come when we as a house are entitled to know more than we do know about the war effort of this country, the commitments that have been made in many phases of our war effort, and other matters closely related to the conduct of the war.
For example I am anxious to know whether we are a partner in this war, or whether we are being relegated to the position of allowing the major powers, if I may so express it, to take the decisions, inform the government of Canada of them and then perchance invite us to conference after the decisions have really been taken and the policy decided upon. I have in mind Casablanca. I have not yet seen the answer given this afternoon to a question I placed on the order paper regarding the Bermuda conference. I am anxious to know whether we are called in in the initial stages, or whether the decisions are usually taken by other nations allied with us, after which, the policy having been more or less decided, we shall be called into conference.
If some of the matters which we have in mind may not be discussed in open session, then an opportunity must be provided to discuss them in a closed session of this house. We want to know what the situation is regarding our armed forces, what the likelihood is for reinforcements and so on during the coming summer months. How adequate are the defences of this country, and1 to what extent are we now relying upon our allies for its defence? To what extent, for example, are we looking after not only our

Canada's War Position
own coastline but the coastline of Labrador and Newfoundland? To what extent are the army, the navy and the air force of the United1 States looking after the vital approaches to this country instead of our own forces?
Also in such a session we should be given a clear understanding of the needs in the realm of exports. There is a good deal of criticism in eastern Canada regarding the piles of equipment to be seen along the railway tracks. People are asking whether this equipment is obsolete, or why it has not been exported. If the government made a statement on the Atlantic situation it would help a great deal in enabling the people to understand the reasons for the piling up of supplies along the railway tracks. There is no secret about it; anyone who takes a trip from Ottawa to Windsor can see literally acres of supplies along the sidings in some of the cities along the way. We ought to be told- also what the food situation is, and what is expected of us. We are being rationed, which is all to the good; and I believe the shortage of food supplies in this country is not serious for Canadians. But to what extent must we make a greater effort to see to it that supplies of food are available for shipment overseas? What is the situation in Great Britain and North Africa and other places regarding food?
Are our ports sufficiently protected? We have never had a clear statement in this house as to that. What about the submarine menace? How is the St. Lawrence to be protected this year? Is the protection to be any better than it was in the previous year? What is the situation on the Pacific coast? To what extent is the Hudson Bay route likely to be used, and how is it protected? Those of us who come from the prairies realize now as perhaps we did not in previous years the accessibility of the prairie region to the Hudson Bay district. What is going on in northwest Canada? We hear about a northwest Pacific organization to develop that country, but we in this house know nothing about these things. A short time ago the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) suggested' that a question put on the order paper by one of my colleagues should be withdrawn, and it was withdrawn because of the intimation that to give the information would not be in the public interest. But subsequently I received from New York a newspaper, the Herald-Telegraph I think it was, from which it is clear that not only the questions that my hon. friend was asking were answered, but that the whole
story of the development in that region was being told in the public press of the United States.
We should get to know what is going on in our country. While the Prime Minister very properly pointed out the other day in connection with the air services that the certain privileges granted1 would be withdrawn at the end of the war, nevertheless we have to bear in mind that it may not be possible to withdraw some of these privileges because something of a vested interest may be established. This parliament as the guardian of the property of the people of Canada ought to know what is taking place. I suppose some of us who try to follow them closely have an inkling as to what is going on, but I feel safe in saying that few members of the house are fully informed as to the situation in the Pacific area, in the Labrador and Hudson bay areas, in the Athabaska region where oil exists, and all across the north country. The house cannot allow itself to be faced with a series of accomplished1 facts, a series of commitments. The other day for the first time we were informed of the great electric power development at Shipshaw, the development of the aluminum plant and so on near Arvida. How many of us in this house knew anything about it until we saw it discussed first of all in the public press and later confirmed by interviews with the ministers? Yet these are the resources of the people of Canada; their alienation will influence the course of events in Canada not only during this war but for generations to come. We are derelict in our duty if we fail to investigate, not after something is done but before it is done, because we are placed here as the trustees of the people and the administrators, if you will, of the common property of this nation.
I suggest therefore that before this house adjourns all the information possible should be given publicly; and if there are matters that cannot be disclosed in public because of the value they would be to the enemy, then a closed session of this house should be held. On Friday the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made a statement which in a measure met with our approval. We were glad to learn that the matter of air transport had been given so much consideration and that certain protection had been given to the Canadian people in connection with transcontinental, international and external air transport. But in my opinion this is not sufficient. We are going to see valuable routes established to the east of the Rocky mountains, and particularly along the outskirts of
Canada's War Position

the Rocky mountains, with the opening up of the great north country. It seems to me we should not allow any vested interests to grow up in connection with projects of this description, particularly in regard to aviation; for after all when we come right down to brass tacks what are we doing? We are providing meteorological services; we are providing airfields, lights, radio, and beacons; then we are going to allow a private corporation to obtain a vested interest in this route. To my mind this is analogous to calling upon our Canadian National Railways to 'lay the railway lines, provide the stations, and then allowing a private corporation to operate their trains over those lines, for which the people of Canada must pay.
We should inquire into some of these matters at the earliest possible opportunity. Perhaps many of the topics to which I have referred can be discussed publicly on various of the estimates, but I want the government and the house to consider which of these subjects, particularly those related to defence, cannot be discussed openly, and before we go back to our constituencies we should be given information regarding many of these matters.
Let me add that before we have a secret or private session of this house it should be well organized. Last year the members of the opposition groups, and perhaps also the government supporters, were asked to submit topics which they thought would be suitable for discussion. Well, we did that, and in their statements the ministers covered those topics fairly well. But in addition to having the ministers answer questions which may be asked in advance by members of this house, an opportunity should be given for further questions to be asked at such a session. We might agree among ourselves that when we meet for a day in secret session we forego the privilege of forty minute speeches and limit the discussion as nearly as possible to short, five or ten minute speeches, if we have to speak, or in the main to questions. In that way we might get the information we desired, but if a private session is held and we have a number of long statements by the ministers, followed by forty minute speeches by two or three members of the house, most hon, members who may have questions to ask will beN denied the privilege of asking them.
I thought I should raise this matter on going into committee of ways and means, because we are perhaps less than two weeks away from the Easter adjournment. We wish to go home to our constituencies, and we shall be asked questions about some of the problems I have mentioned. The sovereign power within this

country ought to be given information upon which members can base answers to the questions that will be asked, provided always-and I am quite sure we can all be relied upon to do this-that we do not divulge matters which in war time ought not to be divulged.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: OPPORTUNITY FOR DISCUSSION OF CANADA'S WAR POSITION-STATEMENT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was unaware that there was to be any debate such as this to-day. I shall be very brief, because we have business before the house at the moment of a practical character that must take precedence over anything that might be regarded as theoretical. I do wish to say, however, that as members of parliament, representing the Canadian people, we must not allow this house to drift into the position of a semi-peacetime parliamentary assembly. After all, this war has reached a stage which I think most of us regard as extremely serious. Speaking in a personal capacity only, I view with considerable approval the suggestions advanced by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) in regard to the matter of a secret session. I think the country would welcome some move by the government to take into its confidence the representatives of the people. Frankly I am alarmed at the feeling throughout Canada that we in this House of Commons are not paying enough attention to the war but are paying too much attention to other things. I should not care to cast the responsibility for this upon any single person in the house, or upon the government or any of the groups, but I believe the people wish that as a parliament we devote our attention first of all to the winning of this war. That is the first thing to be done. No matter what procedure we may adopt in this house from time to time, which to us may seem reasonable and proper, we must also impress upon the people the fact that in this House of Commons the first and major concern of those who sit as the representatives of the people is the winning of the war. More than that, if I may say so, the government should take the peoples' representatives more fully into their confidence. I think that is long overdue and it is something which would be most acceptable to the people generally.
It would be particularly appropriate now, I think, that the government acquaint members of parliament as far as possible with the whole international position. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar omitted to mention a couple of matters which came to my mind as he was speaking. Members of this house should be given some idea of the progress of the battle of the Atlantic. They should be given

Canada's War Position
more complete information with respect to Canada's foreign policy, because for too many people in Canada that matter has not been sufficiently clarified. I am mentioning these points because I have hesitated to hold up the house with motions on going into supply or ways and means. I do wish to caution my hon. friends to the left that one of the biggest jobs we can do at the moment is pay attention to the budget resolutions, and the practical means of giving the government the supply it requires in connection with the war effort.
For that reason I wish to apologize for the brevity of my remarks in this matter, but also to give my approval to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that the people's representatives should be taken more fully into the confidence of the government. May I also say to the government, however, that at the moment our main job is to get on with the business now before the house, so that there shall not be an extended debate, as has been originated this afternoon.
Right Hon. AV. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):	Mr. Speaker, may I say
at once the government has no desire whatsoever to withhold information of importance to the people of Canada, or their representatives in this house. But the business of parliament cannot be carried on without following some procedure which will make it an orderly and expeditious procedure.
In the early part of the session my hon. friend made much the same speech as he has made this afternoon, about the desirability of the house being more fully informed on different matters, and as to our having a secret session in order that information might be given in greater detail. I replied to him at the time, and I give him the same reasons this afternoon. That was on February 26, and Hansard at .pages 732-33 records the discussion as follows:
Mr. M. J. Coldwell (Rosetown-Biggar):	Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Prime Minister. Now that the address in reply to the speech from the throne has been adopted, will he suggest an early date when this house can meet in closed session to discuss matters relating to Canada's part in the war?
Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King (Prime Minister): Mr. Speaker, I am anxious to oblige the house. It is entirely a matter of what is likely best to fulfil the wishes of hon. members and best to further public business. The plan on which the government was proceeding was to bring down as soon as possible our financial measures in toto. The estimates are already down. A resolution with respect to the war appropriation has just been advanced a stage from government notices of motion, and will hereafter appear under orders of the day. There
is also now upon the order paper a resolution respecting the making of war supplies available for the united nations. In this way we have sought to give the house a complete picture of the sums which the government will ask to have appropriated. A request has been made that wre should establish the standing and select committees as rapidly as possible. Until all the committees are set up and until the house has had the preliminary statements -with regard to total expenditures, with the sort of breakdown that my hon. friend the leader of the opposition has asked for, so that hon. members may be able to study the details, I do not think we should interrupt the proceedings in order to hold a secret session. If the situation were so pressing that a secret session to discuss other matters would be regarded as more important than proceeding with the government's financial measures for the war, in the manner I have indicated, I would say that ive -would fix a day for a secret sesison forthwith; but if there is no situation that is being embarrassed by not having a secret session at once I think the house would be in a better position to discuss in secret session matters pertaining to the war after it has had before it a complete picture of the financial situation. It is a matter of balancing. I should be glad to talk it over with my hon. friend and other leaders, if they so desire, and see if we cannot perhaps agree on a time that would be best.
On the following page of Hansard, this further reference was made to the business of the house:
Fifteen committees have already been appointed. There remain the five of which notices are already on the order paper, one of [DOT]which was under discussion yesterday and will continue to be discussed to-day. So that between now and Tuesday evening the first order of business will be the discussion of the setting-up of these different committees. The Minister of Finance proposes to proceed on Wednesday with the motion respecting the war appropriation for the ensuing year, and would like to have the house continue with discussion on that measure unless there are some other matters that it may be necessary to take up in the interval. The minister hopes to be able to make headway with the war appropriation discussion from the time that he proceeds with the resolution in the house.
That indicates the plan under which the government proceeded to bring the important measures before the house at as early a day as possible, so as to permit of the fullest possible discussion by hon. members.
Then, following what was said on that occasion I had a conference with my hon. friends, the leader of the opposition, the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and the leader of the Social Credit party, at which time we all agreed upon a certain programme which, I may say, has been followed literally from that day to the present. The fact that we have not made as rapid headway with the measures to be placed before the house has not been the fault of the government. As my hon. friend is rvell aware-and I am not complaining-there have been some

Canadas War Position
amendments. I wish to make the position of the government perfectly clear in that matter. There have been amendments moved on going into supply and ways and means. There has been extended debate on the budget and other subjects. Those discussions have taken up a great deal of our time, and because of that we have not reached certain of these other measures.
May I point out that in connection with the appointment of special committtees a week of the time of the house was taken up in the discussion of reconstruction and social security. As the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) has just said, I emphasized before that and have since repeated time and again that I thought we were taking up far too much time in the discussion of some measures which were really of a domestic nature, and possibly too much time in the discussion of post-war matters, rather than giving our time, as we should be giving it, in the fullest way, to the discussion of measures such as, the war appropriation bill, and others related immediately to the prosecution of the war.
I am not complaining about the time the house has taken up in discussing some of these matters. I know they were matters of importance. But the reason we have not thus far been able on other matters to give to hon. members of the house some of the information they would like to have is not that we have been planning to withhold it, or that we have been arranging the business of the house so that it might be withheld or delayed. We have made such progress as has been possible in view of the fact that other subjects have come up for discussion.
The leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Coldwell) has said that the government has a responsibility to the people, and that it is not the master but rather the creature of the house. It is because, as leader of the government, I regarded myself as the creature rather than the master of the house, that I sought to get into touch with my fellow creatures who are leading the other parties, in an effort to come to some agreement on the order of business to be followed. I am happy to say we came to an agreement, and I think the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar would be the first to admit that we have followed the order of business set down at that time.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) has succeeded this year in bringing down the budget at an earlier date than it has been brought down in any other year, not only in this parliament, but, I believe, earlier than in almost any session of any other parliament.

The one measure above all others with respect to which the people of Canada were most anxious to get full details was the budget. The business of the government was so far advanced1 that the Minister of Finance was in a position to bring down his budget almost as soon as the debate in reply to the speech from the throne was completed.
Then, the debate on the budget has taken a long time. Had' we withheld the presentation of the budget until after the Easter recess, some of the measures to which my hon. friend has now referred would have been proceeded with. But, as the Minister of Finance has made abundantly clear, there are some commitments which will have to be met within a certain time. In order that those commitments may be met he must get his financial resolutions through the house.
May I say in conclusion that the real reason some of the matters referred) to this afternoon have not been dealt with is that everything cannot be done at one and the same time. The fullest opportunity will be granted hon. members to discuss all measures. When the war appropriation bill is introduced it will undoubtedly be discussed) at great length. But I cannot see any advantage to be gained by seeking to enter into a debate of one or two days so as to supply in brief compass information which the house will wish to have in detail, and which would require two weeks or possibly longer to discuss at length.
I do not wish in any way to indicate a desire to abridge the rights of any hon. member. On reflection however I think it will be seen that the choice lies between agreeing to a plan and following it to as great an extent as possible, or seeking to deal with matters at random and, on that account, less efficiently.

Canada's War Position

I think we are all agreed that the most pressing business of this session is the winning of the war and the doing of everything that will assist the government in attaining that objective. But there are certain things which we feel ought to be discussed, and discussed as soon as possible. We are not quarrelling with the statement of the Prime Minister about having the business of the house conducted in as orderly and expeditious a manner as possible, nor do we quarrel with what he said about the different items that have come up, particularly the budget. We have no difference of opinion on that point at all.
I want to remind the Prime Minister that earlier in the session he said that every hon. member -would have the opportunity on going into supply of discussing any matter which he thought ought to be discussed. This group has taken advantage of that opportunity only once; only one amendment was moved, and the discussion on it took two days. Time is going by. We are not quarrelling with the past; we are simply asking the government to make some commitments with reference to the time between now and the Easter recess. The Prime Minister has made no statement yet about that.
The chances are that there will be a spring offensive. There is a strong likelihood of Canadian troops being in action within weeks or months, and it seems to me that an opportunity should be given, to the defence ministers in particular, to make statements to the house in a closed session. I have been reading the British Hansard for last session and I am amazed at the information which is conveyed to that house in public session. Questions are asked about how a certain tank is performing, whether a mounting has been changed, whether a certain gun has been found satisfactory, if not, what is wrong with it, what is wrong with certain cars, whj'- is their performance not better, and so on. Frank statements are made by the minister. Such a procedure here would strenghten the confidence of the public and of the members of the house. There should be a frank discussion and we should have the opportunity of hearing from the ministers what is being done. Financial measures are important, but to my mind nothing is as important as the lives of young Canadians, many of whom will be going into action within the next few weeks or months. Statements should be made by the defence ministers as to what preparations have been made, what equipment has been put out, what are the arrangements for command, and, above all, what plans have been made for coordination between the services. In many quarters
in this country and in Great Britain there is a feeling of apprehension about the extent of the coordination among the various arms of the service. A statement by the Minister of National Defence as to the facilities that have been set up for coordination of the services would enable hon. members to go back to their constituencies and remove any misapprehension they may have. They could tell their constituents that because of the statements they had heard they now feel that everything that can be done is being done and will be done to make it possible for the Canadian forces to make a maximum contribution to the winning of the war with a minimum of loss.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar was not seeking to criticize the government for not having held a secret session. What he was seeking to do was to point out that time was going by very rapidly. It is unfortunate that in the course of this short discussion the Prime Minister has not said whether or not a day will be set aside before the Easter recess. He should make that statement, if not to-day, certainly in the course of the next few days, in order that members may be able to take back to their constituencies something of the assurance and confidence which would come from the kind of discussion we could have in this house.

That is to say, it may be agreed between the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, the Minister of National Defence for Air and myself that air comes first or navy or army, as the case may be, but the committee will be advised1.
Each minister as his department is taken up is to make a statement regarding the activities of his department. After the statement is made, the estimates or the appropriations of that particular department will be broken down into objects of expenditure, similar to what is done with the estimates we have in peace time. [Mr. Ralston.1
or into matters such as those referred to by my hon. friend. There may be some matters, and he has mentioned very few, which would have to be discussed1 in private. It was agreed between those who met in that conference that every endeavour would be made to complete the consideration of one department before going on with another, although there may be times when it may be necessary or convenient to suspend consideration of one department and take up another temporarily. speechtext:
It is seldom that I am altogether in agreement with the course being followed by the government, but in this matter the course being followed is the one agreed upon. I wish to make this perfectly clear. Speaking for myself alone, I think that instead of having a secret session of the house the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) should from time to time place before the house and the country a statement on the war and Canada's position, making a report similar to that given to the House of Commons in Great Britain by Mr. Churchill. Reports have been given by the Prime Minister from time to time but not as regularly as I think should be the case. To-day we betray no secret in saying that conditions are difficult, indeed terrible, on the Atlantic. The people of Canada do not realize just how serious the conditions are. The mass of war materials that is being produced and piled up, great as it is, can assist the empire at this time only if it finds its way over to the battlefields.
We approach another victory loan campaign which will be an outstanding success if the people know the facts. I feel that all over Canada to-day there is altogether too much apathy, too much of a feeling that the war has been won. What the people of Canada need is a speech from the Prime Minister in which he will give them as nearly as he can within the limits of censorship a true picture of the situation in which we find ourselves to-day. I do not want to play politics, and I say that in all sincerity. It is all very well for us to look at the post-war period. But if parliament, which is one of the custodians of the future of this country and of this empire has half its mind devoted to the war and half to the post-war, we have insufficient of its collective intellect devoted to either. Half of our minds to-day cannot be devoted to helping in the winning of the war and the other half to consideration of the ballot box. Speaking for myself again, I believe-and I think all hon. members are of the same opinion-that the Prime Minister should tell the people of Canada in order to arouse them from their lethargy, the position in which Canada, the empire and the world stand to-day. I do not want to go into a secret session where the information I receive must remain with me. I wish to know, as a citizen of Canada and as a member of this house, what the prospects are, what we are doing toward winning the war,
and whether the mobilization of man-power for service in Canada will aid in winning the war overseas. I wish to know whether the vast amounts of munitions that are being produced in this country are being sent overseas, and generally what we as members can do to assist the government at this time. It is not the government we are assisting by our cooperation; it is all of the people of Canada. It is Canada.

Sir,-I have the honour to inform you that the Right Hon. Sir Lyman Poore Duff, Chief Justice of Canada, acting as deputy of His Excellency the Governor General, will proceed to the Senate Chamber to-day, Monday the 5th April, at 5.45 p.m., for the purpose of giving the royal assent to certain bills.

The house in committee of ways and means, Mr. Bradette in the chair.

Resolved, That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Special War Revenue Act and to provide:
1. That the excise tax on each letter transmitted by post be increased from one to two cents.

Before we proceed, I think we are entitled to an explanation from the Postmaster General or the Minister of Finance, or perhaps both of them, as to the necessity for the increase in the Post Office Department ; and he should put on the record the figures relating to the income and outgo of the department which make it necessary to increase the postage tolls. It is, I think, strange that the grandson of the Postmaster General who was the father of penny postage in Canada should find himself now in the position of abandoning the great principle of penny postage in this country and of raising the postage to the very high rate of four cents.
There is a war on.

Somebody says, "There is a war on". Well, there is such a thing as taxation to the saturation point. I am open to conviction as to the necessity of this increased impost. I have always thought that, in a great public utility like the Post Office Department, the cheaper you make the service the more the public will use it, and that the two will balance. I should like to know if this theory is sound or unsound. I think a four cent postage rate will have the effect of less users of the postal facilities with respect to certain classes of our community, and I hold the view that the increase of this

Special War Revenue Act
tax at this time of high income taxes on corporations and big business firms, and of the excess profits taxes will have the effect of the government paying this tax itself.
Take a company which is in the excess profits tax class, where all its profits over a certain level go to the government as excess profits. Such a company will not care whether the tax is two cents, four cents or ten cents; it will go to the crown, and the very purpose the government has in mind will be defeated. An hon. member has referred to war risk insurance. In this class of insurance, if my memory is correct, forty per cent only of the premium is charged to expense, and the rest has to be absorbed by the company out of its earnings. The same principle applies here. By the way, I might tell the Minister of Finance that I find a great many people in this country are refusing to take up war risk insurance because they regard the rates as being too high. Companies in which I am interested have considered the matter and have deferred from time to time the placing of war risk insurance. This, Mr. Chairman, is just in passing; I do not intend to dwell upon it long. As the danger of invasion becomes remote, so the desire for war risk insurance recedes into the distance. I do not know what was the inception of this demand, but to-day, it seems to me, the whole thing could pretty well be scrapped except in the odd case where certain communities may still have a fear of invasion and destruction.
However, that is not the point I wish to make. I tell the minister that the increased cent in this tax will come from the large corporations, the large business houses, that the cost will come out of the excess profits tax, and that the net income received will be very small. At least, that is the theory on which I am proceeding. I should like to hear the defence of the government in respect to raising the tax. I assume they will say, the increased cost of operating the department. However, I do not know what it will be; we were not told. As I recollect there was just a brief statement in the budget that the rates would be raised, and that was followed by a supplementary statement from the Minister of Finance referring to certain other people. What consideration is the department giving to raising rates on other classes of matter? There are other classes besides first-class matter. What consideration has the government given to raising those rates?
Then the Post Office Department is subsidizing Trans-Canada Air Lines; past experience has shown that the subsidy has been generous, to say the least. The rates at which
mail is being carried by Trans-Canada for this government are on a basis not comparable with rates in the United States. I think the consensus is that the subventions from the Post Office, the public treasury, to Trans-Canada Air Lines are higher than in any other part of the world. They ought to be reduced. We discussed that matter in the railway committee the other day. I am not going into that now. The Postmaster General's illustrious progenitor established penny postage in this country. That will not be his only claim to fame, but it will be one of the chief claims. It was a great achievement. But now we have the sad spectacle of his grandson increasing the postage rates in this country.

speechtext:
The amendment of which I gave notice some weeks ago had better be moved-.
That resolution No. I of the resolutions to amend the Special War Revenue Act be amended to insert the words "and post card" after the words "on each letter" in the first line thereof.
I so move.
This means that the extra cent is an excise tax, not postage?

That is correct. The
postage has not been raised. But my colleague the Minister of Finance has required extra money for the war expenditure. It was estimated that something upwards of $8,000,000 could be raised by an additional one cent on letters and post cards. It was not that the Post Office Department required more money for operating. In fact our surplus as shown in the report has increased substantially in the last few years, from some 83,250 to upward of 84,500,000, with every indication that it will be still higher, although the final figures for the fiscal year are not yet in.
In regard to Trans-Canada Air Lines, the rate is still high, but it has been reduced again this year. Originally it was sixty cents; now it is down to 42-08 cents a mile, I think it is. It has been reduced steadily as the volume of air mail increased. There have been very large increases in air mail. Several years ago it cost the Post Office Department in assistance to the Trans-Canada Air Lines upwards of 8100,000 a month. I am glad to say that during the last year with a thirty per cent allowance for duplication, namely, transfers from one plane to another, and making allowance for mail originating in outside points, for example, United States or Newfoundland, we can show a profit for air operation last year of 8321,000, which is a difference of SI,250,000 to $1,500,000 a year. And the indications are that as far as air mail is concerned those profits will increase.
Special War Revenue Act

The larger part of that profit was made during the last three months of the calendar year, and for January and February the earnings are up greatly over last year, the volume of air mail also being up. So that we are not trying to get additional revenue except for the purpose of assisting the Minister of Finance in financing the war.

Then, instead of the government raising the rates, would it not be in order to leave the rates on. letters as they are but that an excise stamp of one cent be required in addition to the postage? In that way the Post Office Department would have a defence against the charge of advancing the postal rates.

It is unfortunate, but we have to take some of the blame, if any blame should attach to the necessity for raising the money necessary to conduct a war for our very existence. So far as I am concerned I am willing to assume my share. I think the suggestion as to an excise stamp would be wasteful, because it would mean more work. We have post offices all over this country, but in many small places there is no convenient spot where one can go to buy a revenue stamp. My hon. friend will realize what it would mean in the small places and the back concessions in the way of inconvenience to the people. Our postmasters are selling stamps anyway; there is no use in setting up a duplicate system and paying someone in each area to sell revenue stamps. The expense would probably eat up all the income.

The post offices could just as well sell a revenue stamp as a postage stamp. If I were the .minister I would try to defend my department by keeping postal rates where they are. The department shows a surplus. Then, why have that department, which I believe is the only revenue department we have to-day, charged with increasing postal rates? As far as cost goes it would not amount to anything; these revenue stam.ps could1 be .printed at very little extra cost, and the minister's staff could handle the two just as easily as one.
Not just as easily. The whole matter was discussed, and it was thought this was the most convenient way for the public.
All the money goes into one common pool, does it not?

Yes, but the postmasters throughout the country and officials of the

department handle it. Someone would be paid a commission on the sale, or it would be included in their regular salaries and bonuses and charges.

Why
should they not do this extra work for nothing?

That question is under
consideration at the moment.

I suggest
that as a patriotic gesture the postmasters should sell these stamps for nothing. I know a good many of the postmasters have limited incomes, but they all have more than they' did during the depression; most of them are doing quite well now. The discussion seems to indicate that this is a tax, pure and simple, to help out the revenues of the country. What about the point I raised1, that in the final analysis it will defeat its purpose because the big users of the postal services are the large companies, most if not all of whom are within the excess profits tax class and therefore will pay nothing extra. I think that is the true position. Just how much that will amount to I do not know, but I should think it would assume very large proportions. The Postmaster General has suggested that it is hoped $8,000,000 will be raised by this method. How much of that will come from the excess profits tax or the war income taxes paid by these very large companies?

Before the minister
answers that question I should like to ask another one, which sort of joins with it. As I heard the leader of the opposition-

No, not
the leader of the opposition.

Well, the quondam
leader of the opposition. It occurred to me that perhaps the minister might be able to indicate to the committee the amount or the proportion or the percentage of the money coming to the Post Office Department which comes through the sale of stamps to ordinary individuals and businesses that do not have large quantities of mail matter, as compared with the large companies which the hon. member mentioned. Is there any division which the minister could give us. I have often wondered just what share of the revenues of the post office comes from John Doe and Richard Roe, and how much from the very large business concerns mentioned by the hon. member for York-Sunbury. In a sense that is the same question asked by the hon. member, put in a different way.

The hon. member for
York-Sunbury mentioned payments to postmasters. He understands, I am. sure, that they are paid on the basis of the earnings of the previous year.
A commission.; that is the small offices.	-

Yes, on last year's business. I think it is true that the postmasters are receiving better remuneration on the whole than previously, though, mind you, there are some points where for one reason or another there has been a drop in business. There are nob very many of those; on the whole what the hon. member says is substantially correct. But I would also remind him that these postmasters are doing a great deal of work they did not do previously, and in many instances they are doing it to help the war effort.
For which they are not paid.

Yes; they are doing it in order to help out, and I wish to mention that in order to keep the record clear and so that no false impression may get abroad in this connection. They deserve credit for a great deal of the work they have been doing, work they volunteered to do because they desired to help. As far as the financial end of it goes, I will leave that to my colleague the Minister of Finance.

I should like to add just a word to what was said by the Postmaster General in reference to causing the postmasters to do some additional work for nothing. As a matter of fact I am rather surprised at the proposal that was advanced. It is all very well, sitting here in this house, at a moment's notice to take up the time of some other person in the country, with no return. It is all very well to take all the postmasters and say, "Oh, don't pay them for this work. Have them do this work for nothing." In the first place the hon. gentleman suggested that these stamps might be sold in a different way, that there might be a different sort of stamp. In reply to the suggestion that this would involve extra work he answered, "Oh, well, that is all right; have the postmasters do it for nothing." I submit that is an entirely wrong way to proceed and an entirely wrong principle to adopt. I think as a matter of fact people like the hon. member are just a little too ready to ask some other person to do something for nothing. I believe that if the postmasters do a job they are entitled to be paid for it, just as any other person is entitled to be paid for what he does. I am quite sure that if we were passing a law here which required
people to consult lawyers, the hon. gentleman would join with me in opposing any suggestion by a third party that the lawyers should do the work for nothing, and the same thing applies to postmasters. When a man does something he should be paid for it; he is worthy of his hire.

If I may just add a word in connection with the question of postmasters, I think the experience of most hon. members coming from rural districts is that postmasters, as a class, cannot be said to be overpaid. As a matter of fact I have a great deal of sympathy for the average rural postmaster, who in many instances is barely able to eke out an existence. He, together with the rural mail carrier, has a very difficult time to cany on. I am quite sure the remarks of my desk-mate and colleague, the hon. member for York-Sunbury, would not normally be interpreted as anything more than taking part in the discussion of a matter of this kind in an attempt to find the ways and means which will best deal with the situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that puts it on the right basis.

Perhaps the minister will just keep quiet until I have finished. I would just add that I hope the Postmaster General will not ask the postmasters of Canada to do, without some further remuneration, anything more than they are doing now. There are many other people who could much better afford to do something for the war effort-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Name some of them, please; just one.
The Minister of Finance; that was whom I had in mind, and I am glad the minister gave me the opportunity. I do feel that as far as the rural people are concerned-
Would the hon. member permit a question?
No, I will not. In respect of postmasters generally in Canada, I wish to repeat that the minister should be very careful before giving them extra work to do, without some extra remuneration.

I thought I had made it clear that in many instances these postmasters, through their organizations, had volunteered to assist in the war effort-and to do this work without any additional expense. I do not want anyone to get the impression that we are trying to load the postmasters down with all sorts of extra work without extra pay. They do get a commission on unemployment insurance stamps, but they are doing
Special War Revenue Act

a great deal of extra work in connection, with the war, work they have volunteered to carry on.

That is
exactly what I had in mind, though of course the politically-minded hon. member for Winnipeg South-Centre sought to place upon what I said an interpretation that I had not in mind at all.
Will the minister just tell us what commissions are paid on the stamps sold through the post offices? Let me say at once that on the great majority of the postage stamps sold in this country no commission is paid. They are sold through the big city offices, and at a minimum. The practice of giving commissions to rural postmasters is to help them eke out their salaries. I should think it is an unsatisfactory practice, and one which would lead to a certain amount of evasion. If a man is performing a service as postmaster he ought to be paid a decent wage for his services, irrespective of the revenues collected by his office. To-day in the smaller offices they receive salaries. But no one could live on $100-and I can remember when it was $35. Then, in addition they receive commissions from the sale of stamps. We might be surprised if we were to learn how high that commission percentage is. Although the volume is not large, the percentage is very high.
Usually this work is done purely as a sideline. No one could accept the job as the work of a lifetime, or as a full-time job, in a small community. In the larger communities the postmaster is paid a salary, and I believe that salary is gauged by the revenue from the office. The amount of commission does not mean so much to him. As a rule these postmasters are paid a certain stipend, out of which they pay their help. That is a situation which, in my opinion, ought to be reviewed. What control has the Postmaster General over the pay a postmaster gives his help? I know of one instance where the poor assistant does nearly all the work and gets a pitifully low salary. Surely that is not a satisfactory situation. I have in mind one particular example in which the postmaster in a small town receives $3,200. He has an assistant, and I venture to say that the assistant puts in more hours of work than the postmaster, but is paid only $800 a year. I do not see how a man could live on it. However, that is the bargain between the postmaster and his assistant, and I do not suppose the Post Office Department has anything to say about it.
Will the minister tell the committee what commissions are paid on the sale of postage

stamps? How much of this extra cent does he anticipate will be taken up in commissions? I do not think the proportion will be very large, because the great bulk of stamp sales is to the big commercial houses, where no commissions are paid, the expenses coming out of operating expenses. This is an instance where a tax is pulled out of the hands of one tax-gatherer and placed into the hands of another tax-gatherer.

I think the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) will agree that the latter part of his observations, with respect to the payment of employees in post offices, might better be dealt with when the estimates for the Post Office Department are before the committee.
Yes; I was just pointing out the iniquity of it.

So far as percentages are concerned, I may inform the committee that on amounts up to $1,000 they receive seventy per cent; thirty per cent in excess of $1,000 and up to $10,000; and in excess of $10,000 up to $20,000 they receive twenty per cent, plus commissions on money orders and postal notes.
That means in a small post office that seven-tenths of this increase of a cent will go in commissions.
No; that is not correct.
Then I do not understand what the minister has said.

The hon. member asked what the present rate was. Previously he had asked whether the postmasters would receive increased commissions. He had made the suggestion that the postmaster should not receive anything on the extra cent.

I did not make that suggestion. I suggested that the postmasters might do it as a patriotic gesture. I asked the minister if he had given consideration to it, and he said they were already considering it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should think everyone would try to associate himself with that suggestion; it is a very good one.

It has
some merit, of course; it would not have come out of my brain, if it had not merit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
One of the most amusing incidents I can remember has been 'the display of nervous anxiety and haste with which the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), the leader of the opposition, rushed in to try to place the matter before the committee

Special War Revenue Act
before the information went out that his seat-mate was going to ask postmasters to do the work for nothing. As a matter of fact I do not think there is much more work, if any. I am certainly in favour of treating postmasters justly, but I would expect that very careful consideration would be given to any proposal to increase their remuneration by virtue of their larger tax revenue.
The postmasters are divided into two groups, the first of which consists of civil servants paid by parliamentary appropriation. This group covers the most important post offices, and about seventy-five per cent of the total postal revenue comes from it. They do not derive commissions from the sale of stamps.
The second group consists of so-called revenue post offices, the postmasters receiving commissions from the sale of stamps, on a graduated basis. As the Postmaster General has said, if stamp sales are 81,000 or less the commission is seventy per cent. To the extent that stamp sales exceed $1,000 and do not exceed $10,000, the commission is thirty per cent; and on sales of stamps in excess of $10,000 the commission rate is twenty per cent. It is clear that a very small percentage of total stamp sales bear the seventy per cent commission rate.
But the amount paid a postmaster in 1943 is not based upon 1943 sales. It is based upon the sales in 1942. What they will receive in 1944 for their 1943 sales remains to be decided. That is under consideration by the Post Office Department. If they consult me about it, I shall bring forward the suggestion of the hon. member for York-Sunbury, if he has not backed away from it.

I do not care who is the father of it. Let us approach the matter realistically,- and not try to make political capital out of it. The fact remains that in any of the post offices with revenues of $1,000 or less, seventy per cent of the increase, if given effect to in 1944 on the basis of 1943 revenue, will go to the postmaster. And very little of it, as a result, will go to the winning of the war. That is statement No. 1.
In post offices where the revenue exceeds $1,000 and does not exceed $10,000, seventy per cent of the first thousand goes to the postmaster, and thirty per cent, or nearly a third, of the excess. In those cases nearly a third of the total accumulated from this one cent will not go to the winning of the war. That is not good enough. This is a war tax. Let us do something to work it
out so that it will go to the winning of the war, and not into somebody's pocket.
We have heard the statement many times that we are not to make profits out of this war. Here in a small way, and covering a multitude of small transactions, the government can give effect to that principle. I am standing by that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I agree with that.

I should like to make a suggestion to the Postmaster General and to the Minister of Finance, because it seems he has to give consent before suggestions of this kind can be accepted. My suggestion is that all our men and women in uniform overseas be given the franking privilege. Those who are overseas are making great sacrifices for the rest of us On this side of the water, and it would be a proper gesture on our part to extend the franking privilege to them. I am not referring to letters alone. I am referring also to parcels that are sent overseas. I understand that it costs, on an average, $5 to send one of these parcels, and to many of the families of the men and women receiving them $5 is a large amount. I understand that the actual cost of sending a parcel over is around $1.30, and I suggest that the Minister of. Finance look for some other source of revenue and institute free franking privileges for mail overseas.

I wish to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. I do not think postmasters in the villages and smaller towns are overpaid, especially when we consider the increase in the cost of living. I know of several cases where postmasters have taken a loss. They must pay the rent of their premises and also the wages of any help they need.

They get no cost-of-living
bonus.

Their cost of living has
gone up and they get no bonus. I know of four or five postmasters in my district who are rendering a wonderful service. They have headed up the different loan and salvage campaigns. The postmaster in my town headed up a campaign which collected two carloads of old tires. When he was doing that work he had to hire help for the post office. The same postmaster has headed up the last two victory loan campaigns, and I am sure he will do the same thing again. I wish to make a plea on behalf of these men and ask that they not be put to any extra expense. This is the life business of many of these men. The postmaster in my town has held this position since

Special War Revenue Act

he returned from the last war. He has a war disability, but he is doing a wonderful job. He is making this his life work. These men are certainly not overpaid. I was about to suggest something along the line of that suggested by the hon. member for Battle Creek (Mr. Fair), that some reduction be made in the cost of sending letters to men overseas. I do not think it is quite fair that these letters should have to pay this extra cost.
The hon. member is referring to what letters?
Letters going to men overseas.

As the minister has pointed out, everything that has been said so far might better be said on the post office estimates. The main thing we have to deal with now is whether or not this is a proper war tax. If we believe it is, then we should pass it, and everyone should be willing to pay his share of the tax. There is one thing I like about the Minister of Finance-it is not the only one-he has the courage to stick to an unpopular thing when he once sees it is necessary. I only hope that on this occasion his courage is contagious. The hon. member for York-Sunbury is not in his seat at the moment, and I am wondering whether he is not the same member who a few moments ago waxed so eloquent over the statement made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and said, "Let us get on with the war." Whenever two cents are being discussed, the hon. member for York-Sunbury will be found haggling about them, where they are going and what they are going to do. As far as I am concerned I am willing to pay my share of the increased postage and my share of any other tax, without complaining in any way.

I have had considerable experience with the smaller post offices, and I agree with the hon. member for Qu'Appelle in what he says about the service they are giving. I tried to have the salaries of some postmistresses and postmasters increased, and I did not fail in every case. I have often wondered how they were able to keep up their homes on such small salaries. I have found that many people using these smaller post offices buy their stamps in the city. That is not fair. I think the Postmaster General should try to find some way by which the local post offices get the benefit of the commission on the sale of stamps.

As I understand it, the purpose of this amendment is to secure more revenue for the national treasury; it is not to

afford an opportunity to discuss whether postmasters are receiving enough salary. It does not take any more effort on behalf of a postmaster to sell a four-cent stamp than it does to sell a two-cent stamp, and he receives a little more revenue. The suggestion has been made, and I think it is a good one, that the new stamp should indicate that the increase is not an increase in postage rates but is an excise tax in addition to the postage for the purpose of getting more revenue. I think the four-cent stamp could be so designed to indicate that the postage is three cents, and the excise, one cent. That would indicate to the general public that an excise tax of one cent was being collected for war purposes. They would not be likely to think that the post office was going behind as a result of its war activities and that it was necessary to increase the rate 25 per cent. I suggest that the Postmaster General give this his consideration.
I would point out that the postage is two cents and that the tax will now be two cents. The new stamp will bear the portrait of his majesty in uniform and will be available about April 15.

The hon. member for
York-Sunbury raised) the question as to how much of this additional revenue would be new revenue, and how much might be chargeable as an expense on various companies that paid either forty per cent or eighty per cent of their income as taxation. That was followed up by a question by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre asking if the Post Office Department knew' how' much of the mail emanated from private individuals and how much from business organizations. Can the minister throw any light on these two points?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is no accurate estimate of the proportion of the mail that is business mail. A very substantial proportion is non-business mail. The best estimates would run from one-third to one-half for non-business mail. With regard to the business mail the postage is deductible as a business expense. The businesses would be either those operating at a loss or those operating at a profit and paying forty per cent on their profits in combined income and excess profits taxes, or paying what amounts to eighty per cent; that is, one hundred per cent with twenty per cent returnable. I have spoken of businesses that were corporations. There are different rates for those that are not corporations. There is also a different rate for small businesses, a thirty per cent rate.

how much is net gain?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, we have not.
You have figured the gross?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. There is an estimate
here of $8,000,000, but it is only an estimate; it may be $9,000,000 or something like that. We are making some allowance for some diminution in letter sending, but are not making any allowance for diminution of income and excess profits taxes. We had the same difficulty when we imposed other excise taxes. The tax on soft drinks, for example, may result in a company leaving the price to the consumer the same and paying the tax on a very much smaller profit, unless some steps are taken. I do not know what steps have been taken with regard to soft drinks, but I think steps were taken to offset that eventuality. The possibility is always there, that an excise tax will be assumed by the person on whom the tax is imposed to the prejudice of the income tax revenue. Undoubtedly the income tax revenue will suffer to some extent. With some companies, thirty per cent of the postage will come out in income taxes, with others, forty per cent; with others, fifty per cent, and nothing in the case of some companies. With regard to unincorporated proprietors I do not know what the percentage would be. It may be fifteen per cent. We just have to realize that there will be some diminution of income tax revenues.

The minister expects he will get a net of $5,000,000; would that be a fair estimate? While I am on my feet, I understand that the hon. member for Vancouver East read me a lecture a few moments ago. He has gone from the chamber. He shoots and runs. I am not in the habit of shooting and running. He said that I was concerned about winning the war, which I am, and I think very much more than, he is. Then he said I get into a discussion of a two-cent item with respect to the war effort.
If this opposition does not take an intelligent interest in the discussion of these budget resolutions I wonder who in this house will. Will it be the hon. member for Vancouver East? Will it be any member of his group? How much help have they given to elucidating some of the perplexing problems that have arisen in budget resolutions in days gone by? I have conceived it my duty within the limit of my capability to try to get to the public the
elucidation of some of these resolutions. I find it difficult to understand many of them. We are coming to one of the resolutions that I have not yet been able to fathom, and I have had the assistance of officers from the income tax department. How much light shall we get from the hon. member for Vancouver East on that point? He is much more concerned about making a political point against a political opponent than he is about the war or anything else.

In regard to the airmail rate, which will now be seven cents as against six cents, while many of us have sympathy for a certain number of users of the mail, people whose incomes are very low, who will have to pay four instead of three cents, I believe that those who are accustomed to use airmail and are now paying six cents can well afford to-pay not merely seven cents but ten cents. I would ask the minister how much the one-cent increase in the airmail rate will mean in revenue, and from that we can figure out what an increase of four cents to a ten-cent rate would have made. Just what reasons entered into the minister's consideration in raising the airmail rate from six to seven cents? The figures indicate that the poundage of airmail carried in this country has been growing by leaps and bounds. The companies which use airmail can well afford to spend ten cents in place of the proposed rate of seven cents, and those who use the mail for personal reasons can well afford to pay an extra four cents instead of the extra one cent proposed.

I do not agree with the hon. member's attitude in regard to a further increase in the price of airmail. The Post Office Department has to pay the money to operate the Trans-Canada Air Lines, so far as the postal operation is concerned, and we want it to be a paying and not a losing proposition. I am speaking for myself and, I believe, for the officials of the department. We have got it out of the red. We were losing about $1,300,000 a year, and now we are operating at $321,000 profit. I think we can stand the one-cent increase, but if the increase were more than that I should not like to say how much the volume would decrease. We have to pay on a per-mile basis regardless of whether the planes carry one pound, one hundred pounds or seven hundred pounds. Our idea is to get those planes carrying the maximum amount of mail they are able to carry. If they carry the maximum we make money. If not, it costs the post office and the taxpayers of this country money. I cannot agree with the hon. member.

I think it would be bad business to increase the rate further and it would mean a drop in /olume. I know the hon. member's attitude in regard to airmail. If I am correct he suggested at one time that we should give consideration to cutting off the service west of Winnipeg during the war.

The minister is quite
WTong. I am simply asking for the considerations that entered into his mind in determining on this increase, whether it should be one cent, three cents, ten cents or anything else. I want to know the facts on which the resolution is based.
On the other point, I never suggested that airmail service from Winnipeg to the west should be discontinued. What I did say at one time, and I still say it, is that when Great Britain was fighting the nazi aeroplanes and there were insufficient bombers available, our Trans-Canada Air Lines here saw fit to expand its air services, and I saw advertisements on every mail truck in the country advocating that people use the airmail because it was faster; endeavouring to increase the load, to use more gasoline and to use more aeroplanes when they were very badly needed overseas. At the present time the situation has, I think, somewhat ameliorated. Nevertheless this committee is entitled to know what considerations entered into the minister's mind when he advocates a seven-cent rate as against ten cents.

The resolution is to increase by one cent the tax on letters. Letters, whether they go by surface, by rail or by air, are still letters, and the one cent goes on them. I do not see any reason why there should be a discrimination against airmail.
The minister has to raise the revenue if he can.

Airmail is a profitable undertaking; it is increasingly profitable every year. The reason why I object is that I think, if my hon. friend's suggestion were followed, it would not be a profitable undertaking; I think it would probably be a losing undertaking, because there would be too large a differential between the price of sending a letter by air and that of sending it by train.

There is one other feature with regard to airmail which should not be overlooked. This dominion is several thousand miles wide, and nothing has done more to make the coastal areas of Canada feel that they are part of Canada than the airmail and the air service. I fear I must disagree with the hon. member for Rosedale. It may

not mean much in getting mail from Toronto _ to Ottawa, but certainly it has meant wonderful things for the people of the Pacific coast, particularly the business people, to be able to get their mail back and forth overnight. It would be very unfortunate if this tax were made higher than one cent. I think the Postmaster General is quite right in his view that it should remain at one cent.

I find
myself in agreement with the hon. member for Vancouver South. But is not this the principle?	I do not know whether it ' is
applicable; I am in an inquiring mood at the moment. When you give a service which is a better service-and an airmail in certain situations is a better sendee than the regular mail service-is it not therefore worth more to the user of the service?
I am not in the position of the hon. member for Vancouver South. An airmail service would not help me to communicate with my constituency; it would mean a delay, because the mail would have to go to Moncton and around a long circuit, so that I never employ it for my own personal use between here and Fredericton. The airmail does not benefit us at all. But is it a sound .principle that because you have a better, a more expeditious service, you are entitled to ask more?
Is that the principle on which this excess is based; or is it on what the traffic will bear?
I do not know. Of course I realize this is an excise tax. I must say I did not have that clearly in my mind when I rose to speak this afternoon. Since it is an excise . tax it does not bear much relation to the question of the transportation of the mail. But there is a principle there to which I have referred which may have some bearing.

The question of airmail rates is one in respect of which our department has kept in touch with the United States postal department, and they with us. Their rate was six cents; our rate has been six cents; and in 1931, I believe, when the tax was changed the one cent was absorbed at that time in the airmail but not in the others. You remember you put the one cent revenue tax on, I think probably on account of the desire to keep the airmail stamps of the same value on each side of the line.
That is one reason.

That is one reason. The second reason is that, I think, over a period of time-not in war time, but as things straighten away-the cost of airmail will

The Royal Assent
definitely be reduced. It all depends upon the matter of income. If the hon. member for York-Sunbury will help to convince the hon. member for Rosedale of the importance of increasing the volume of airmail, we should be able to get that done when the war is over.

The Trans-
Canada Air Lines base their charges on the principle of mileage, do they not?
We pay the Trans-Canada Air Lines on the basis of the miles flown.

That is a more exact way of putting it. You pay the Trans-Canada Air Lines on the basis of miles flown, whether the planes carry one letter or a million letters. They do not do that in the United States, do they? Is it not on the basis of weight?
Both. All kinds of ways.
What is the standard basis on which air carriers are paid in the United States?
In this country we are allowed 1,200 pounds on a plane.
That is the maximum?
Yes, up to 1,200 pounds. In the United States their rate is different. It is based on distance and weight.
Is the airmail rate all over Canada six cents on ordinary letters?
Yes.
It will be seven cents?
Yes.

I have a recollection that I recently sent some mail to Hudson Hope. I was informed that it would be taken by air as far as Fort St. John, and I think I added extra postage for it to be taken on to Hudson Hope. I suppose the difference was accounted for by the mail having to be carried out by stage?
If my hon. friend will give me particulars I will look into the matter and let him know. Perhaps he is mistaken about that.
On the old rate of six cents for airmail, was one cent of that for excise tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will give my understanding;
if I am wrong I shall be corrected. My understanding is that, of the six cents, two cents is postage; three cents, service charge, and one cent, excise tax. That makes up the six cents.
That is on the six-cents basis?
Yes.
That means that on airmail the carrying charge will be only five cents, and two cents will be excise tax?
Yes.
Would the minister let us know how much one cent increase in the airmail rate means in the total revenue?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Seventy-five to one hundred thousand dollars.

I do not suppose that the matter of postage enters into the cost-of-living index. This increase in the postage rate all through the scale is virtually a sales tax on a service, namely, the postal service. I understand from the remarks of the minister on the budget that he does not believe in the principle of an increase in the sales tax. But is this not carrying out the contrary view, that this is simply an increase in sales tax on an essential service? If it entered into the cost-of-living index, I assume the minister would not have been an advocate of the increase in the postal rate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know. I do not think it enters into the cost-of-living index; I am not sure. Whether I would have been investigating it if it had, I do not know. But it would have affected it very little.
