Before recess we were dealing with some matters affecting the Postmaster General. Does this extra cent affect air mail sent overseas to the troops? I received a return from his department which stated that last October thirty per cent of the air mail overseas was sent by boat. I believe during December, 1942, about thirty-four per cent of the Christmas air mail went by boat. I wonder if, at ten cents a letter, he can say how much money would have been paid by the senders of that mail.
In view of the fact that mail from soldiers comes to this country postage free, will the government consider allowing mail going to the soldiers overseas to travel postage free? If so, can the minister give us an estimate of how much revenue would be lost by the government if this were permitted? After all, the troops overseas certainly like to receive mail, and if mail were sent free from this side it might mean as much to them as the sending of mail free to this country.

The one cent does not apply to air mail going overseas to the troops.
In regard to the other questions asked by the hon. member, I believe he will agree that they are matters which might more properly be discussed under post office estimates. If the hon. member would agree, I would be prepared to have them discussed at that time at some length, and on that occasion I could give the fullest information.
What about the last question?

The hon. member mentioned the percentage of air mail going overseas. I wish to make it clear that that does not apply to airgraphs. To my knowledge there have been no airgraphs sent by surface; they have all gone by air. There have been conditions in the Atlantic, which the hon. member will understand, which caused diffi-

culties in connection with the heavy mails at the Christmas season. People who tried to get their mail overseas ahead of time mailed some time in advance, with the result that there was an accumulation. It was thought it would be delayed for months and months if we tried gradually to work out the surplus that had accumulated. The only way was to move it quickly. The Postmaster General of Great Britain made that statement when I was over there. As a matter of fact we discussed the matter together. They had the same problem about that time, with the result that they had to ship several tons of mail by surface to Canada. Those are things which, although unfortunate, cannot be helped.
May I assure the hon. member that officials of the department are doing everything possible to move the mails, and especially air mail. We have asked the public not to use ordinary air mail to England, under the 30-cent rate, until further notice, because only a very small proportion of it can be handled at the present time. The service is practically suspended.
Can the minister say how much revenue would be lost if mail were sent overseas to the troops free of postage?
I should not like to give that at the present time, but I shall get the information for the hon. member. My figures are not sufficiently extensive to give an accurate answer.
Has the government given this matter serious consideration?
Yes; it has been and is being given consideration. So far, however, in view of the demands of war and the need for finances it has not been felt possible to do so.

Just one further question, and I shall have finished with this item. This afternoon I referred to the fact that this tax is a tax on first-class matter only. The government needs the money, and that is the reason for the tax. It must have general revenues to carry on the war. What consideration has been given to the placing of a tax on other classes of matter?

Consideration was given to the placing of taxes on other classes of matter. But, in respect of third-class matter, for instance, the Postmaster General does not have a monopoly in the handling of it in the same way as he has a monopoly in respect of first-class matter. If the rates were raised beyond certain levels people could operate

Special War Revenue Act
agencies for delivery in competition with the Post Office Department. This is not thought to be desirable. We have gone into the whole matter with the Minister of Finance and officials of his department, and it was considered inadvisable to make a change, because if the rates were raised it might involve a loss of business, and the setting up of a duplication of services.

That seems to be sound. Will the additional cent on drop letters, bringing the rate to three cents, not have the effect of diminishing the service in a given area-say a city of 10,000? It can be done much cheaper than 3 cents by hand delivery. Has consideration been given to this matter?

Yes; it was considered. I believe I have heard the hon. member say on many occasions that there is a limit beyond which we cannot go in taxation. In some areas there will be a drop in volume. It will be very difficult to estimate how much is due to the increase in postage, because off-setting that drop there is still an increase in ordinary business. It is hard to tell whether the ordinary business increase will be greater than the drop in the volume. In some places it will not be felt. It will affect the volume to only a very limited extent; at least, that is the feeling of the department. In any event when the postage is raised the volume is cut down to some extent, although I do not think anyone can say exactly how much. The best they can do is to make an estimate based on past results. However, the conditions of this war are rather different. There seems to be considerably more money changing hands and flowing throughout the great body of the people. For that reason it is hard to say whether this diminution of business will be as great as it was when postage was increased in the past.

I suppose
it is a matter of speculation.
Absolutely.

Will the open letters
which were one cent be two cents under the new schedule?

If an open letter contains
printed matter, the rate will be one cent for two ounces; if it contains correspondence, the rate will be four cents, whether the letter is open or not.
Where a circular typewritten letter is sent out at present under the one-cent rate, will it be two cents under the new schedule?

No; it will be one cent
for two ounces.

A
penalty is imposed if the proper postage is not put on a letter. Would it not be wise not to impose this penalty, say for a month? Some people do not understand that additional postage should be put on.

The only result would be that the act would not come into effect as of April 1; it would come into effect as of May 1, as far as any practical application is concerned. If people knew that there was to be no penalty attached, they might possibly continue to use the old rate of postage for the month.

I
know of one firm that had to pay $1.70 this morning for letters that came in without the proper postage attached. There will be other people in the same position, and I was just wondering if that could not be settled.

2.	That the excise tax on cigarettes be increased from one cent to two cents for each five cigarettes or fraction of five cigarettes contained in any package of cigarettes manufactured or imported into Canada.

As one who does not
smoke cigarettes, perhaps I can put in a word for the soldier who smokes. I understand that until recently the soldier could buy in the canteen twenty-five cigarettes for thirty cents, whereas the public had to pay thirty cents for twenty-two cigarettes. With the new tax the soldier will receive twenty-five cigarettes for thirty-five cents, while the public will receive twenty-two cigarettes for thirty-five cents. In view of the limited return received by the soldier, I was wondering if the government would not forgo this tax increase on cigarettes sold in canteens to soldiers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would be difficult to administer without abuse.

I suppose the soldier
might buy for somebody else. However, the soldier receives so little for what he does that it does not seem very much to ask that he be granted the privilege of buying cigarettes at the same price as he paid previously. I presume there is a good deal of revenue received under the present price. I have not the figures at hand', but I am informed that in Newfoundland the situation is much more favourable for the soldier, and that it is still more favourable in the United States. It looks to
Special War Revenue Act

me as though the Canadian soldier is being more or less penalized. After all, the government will receive only a little extra revenue through this increased tax on cigarettes sold to soldiers at the canteen. I think it would be better to go without this revenue because, if that were done, it would certainly leave a much better taste in the soldier's mouth.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To do what the hon. gentleman suggests would be to assert a principle which we have not in our taxation system, that is, that goods sold to members of the forces in Canada should pay no tax.
There is a differential now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not in tax, in price. The forces in Canada get the benefit of the wholesale price. I think the hon. gentleman's figures are correct, although I cannot confirm them. We have not adopted the principle of exempting the members of the forces in Canada from taxes generally.

The
British did long ago. Even in ordinary times you could buy cigarettes on board a British war vessel practically free of taxes, and the same principle applied to ships under British registry. I think the United States government has adopted the same principle with respect to members of their armed forces; I understand they collect very little in taxes on cigarettes.

The same applies to Canadian troops overseas. For instance, our soldiers in Newfoundland are able to buy cigarettes which have paid no tax in Canada. The same applies to our navy and our troops in England. Cigarettes and tobacco can be sent to these men on which no tax is paid in this countiy.
Why is a distinction made between the volunteer undergoing his basic training in Canada and the man overseas?
When goods are exported a refund of the tax can be claimed. That regulation applies not only to tobacco and cigarettes sent to the troops; it applies to all tobacco and cigarettes exported.

How is the excise tax on manufactured tobacco collected and what revenue does the minister expect to get from the new tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The revenue from the tax on manufactured tobacco is estimated at about $14,500,000 for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1943, and it is estimated that the revenue this year from the increase will amount to about $6,500,000.
Does the same principle that applies to cigarettes being sent overseas to our armed forces apply as well to tobaccos?

What was the revenue last year from this tax, and what revenue does the minister expect from this increase this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On cigarette paper and cigarette paper tubes, taking them both together-
That is including resolutions 5 and 6?

6.	That the excise tax on cigarette paper tubes be increased from twelve cents for each one hundred cigarette paper tubes or fraction thereof to fourteen cents.

How is the tax collected on raw tobacco that is used for the manufacture of cigarettes, pipe tobacco and cigars? At what point do you actually do the collecting? The reason why I ask is that one of the large companies had, I understand, to resort to public financing in order to pay the tax. Has there been any complaint in regard to that aspect of levying the tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The manufacturer buys the stamps and puts them on the packages of cigarettes or tobacco before he sells them. That practice has always existed. It means, as the hon. gentleman suggests, that a lot of

Special War Revenue Act
money is tied up, and the higher the tax the more money is tied up. There has been a great deal of complaint about that. We expect to afford some relief in the bill.
The bill will afford some relief?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We expect it to. The amounts that have to be obtained and be kept idle, tied up, are so great that the increase in the tax is becoming a hardship.
How much time elapses between the time the company buys the stamps and the time it actually retrieves the tax from the public?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Around a month is the
average.
What is proposed to be done for such companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The tax is to be treated in the same way as the sales tax. The sales taxpayer has until the end of the following month in which to pay the tax. I am not just clear what part of the amount of this is going to apply to, because it has been so long since these resolutions were prepared. There are, I believe, two kinds of taxes. I shall have to straighten out my information on that because it has been a long time since I looked into it. But the increase this year and perhaps the increase last year will be treated as a sales tax rather than as money that has to be paid for stamps in advance.

On prim ciple, why should there be any difference? The manufacturer or whoever it is who buys the stamps to-day is in the position of having to lay out capital, real money, to buy the stamps, and the government gets the money immediately. The manufacturer takes all the risk of destruction and loss, and he cannot recoup himself until he actually sells the product. Even then he takes some chance on credit sales, if there be any such. He bears the whole load. In the case of the sales tax the manufacturer or whoever it is from whom the department collects does not have to put up any real money until the end of the month in which he makes the sale. Then he is accountable for the sales tax. That seems to be an equitable principle. If you are to give the manufacturer relief on these last two increases why should he not have relief on the whole thing and not be called upon to do other than if it were a sales tax? That seems to me the fair thing to do. Then he would not have to invest and keep idle capital on which he gets no return.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The increase of this year and the increase of last year were taxes. The former imposts were duties.
A distinction without a difference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is a great difference between duties and taxes.
I have heard the Prime Minister argue that all duties were taxes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: From the point of view of administration the difference is this. I am talking now, not about customs duties at all, but about excise duties and excise taxes. Excise duties must be paid before the goods are disposed of.
That is just the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The excise man has existed for centuries. He is an historic figure.
A pretty harsh man, too, as a rule in history.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The excise man is standing right there, and he does not take the lock off or let the goods out until the crown gets the duty. That is an excise duty. Business and industry is accustomed to that, and rightly so. But we have now got ourselves into the position that these imposts, with the increases, are pretty high. We will regard them as duties up to a certain level, but beyond that we are going to regard them as a tax. There is one beautiful thing about duties. You have no bad debts. You cannot have, because you do not let the liquor loose until you get the money.

The
crown does not have any bad debts in either case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, yes, it does. We are in the courts trying to collect sales tax and have a pretty good collection record. The crown has to struggle just like anybody else to collect the taxes.
After all these taxes go on, what will be the total tax on 100 cigarettes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Ten dollars a thousand, which would be a dollar a hundred.
That is, all the taxes added together?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is sales tax in addition.

Is that a dollar a hundred, altogether?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not including the sales tax.
That is eight per cent.
That is just a cent apiece?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Would the minister explain how he expects to collect the excise tax on raw leaf. Apparently it is a new impost.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, it is not.
It is not spoken of as an increase.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is new to this act, because this is a case where we must not get the duty too large; we must place ourselves in a position to allow the manufacturers to finance. It is new to this act, but it is not a new tax. It is half a cent an ounce as against a cent an ounce for the manufactured tobacco. The practice to date has been this, that stamps are sold to what are called packers; they put the stamps on the raw leaf-" hands," they call them

and that stamp must be affixed before the tobacco is sold to the person who uses the raw leaf tobacco.
I am thinking of those smokers who go into a store and buy a "hand" for themselves and break it up and smoke it. Do they escape?

speechtext:
It is stamped before the
storekeeper buys it from the packer.
Oh, it is put on there.

7.	That the excise tax on the price of admission to certain places of entertainment be increased from twenty to twenty-five per cent.

I have had a number of representations from the sixteen picture show operators in my riding. I know very well that the government has to have money. Last year strong representations were made by motion-picture operators; and I have been wondering, in view of the statement made at that time that the increased tax would force a number of picture shows out of business, whether the government has any record of how many have ceased operation since this time last year.
What I have heard and observed convinces me that the picture shows are doing splendid work, in the middle of a very serious war, to maintain the morale of the people. I know of no other agency more effective for this purpose. On Saturday afternoons large numbers of children with their mothers go to see the

shows, and seemingly it strengthens these women to carry on the work they are doing while their husbands are away in the army. The question is, whether this increased tax on picture shows will do more harm than good.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is not increased. The
increase is not on motion-picture shows; it is on night clubs, places of entertainment other than motion-picture shows.
Of course it is not so stated in the resolution, but the bill will be limited to night clubs?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
That puts quite a different complexion on the matter.

There is nothing in the
resolution pertaining to "other than."

It says
"certain places of entertainment," but they are not enumerated.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think I made it clear in
the budget speech.
I had forgotten that. Will the minister give us the reference in the speech?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is at page 861 of Hansard, at the top of the second column:
The amount of expenditures by the public in night clubs and similar places of entertainment seems to me to warrant an increase in the tax on such expenditures and I shall recommend that the rate be raised from 20 per cent to 25 per cent.

I will
vote for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Davenport asked what the effect of the twenty per cent tax on moving-picture establishments had been. I do not think it has had an adverse effect at all. There are some small places in Canada where theatre owners appear to be having a hard time, but my opinion is that it is due almost wholly to causes other than the tax. It is due to the fact that gasoline restrictions make it a little more difficult for people to drive in from the country, or that most of the young men have enlisted and gone away or have gone to work in the war plants. At the same time, every year before the budget we do get representations in favour of a reduction of the tax on motion-picture theatres. I recall clearly the tremendous pressure which was exerted at the time this tax was put on and the. predictions of ruin and disaster which were voiced by those who made these representations. I do not think

Special War Revenue Act
I was ever subjected to more intense pressure than I was by the delegation which urged that the twenty per cent tax on admissions to motion pictures would1 ruin theatres all over the country, and an attempt was made to persuade me to lower that tax from twenty per cent to five per cent. The delegation was accompanied by able counsel, and the members of the delegation were themselves gentlemen of great ability, great persuasiveness and great determination. I am very glad that after a couple of days of this stimulating atmosphere I still was able to say it would remain at twenty per cent.
You met them head-on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. And needless to say
the predictions of lessened attendance did not materialize. Even in the province of Quebec, which unlike Ontario has a very large provincial tax, perhaps fifteen per cent, making a total, if I am correct in that figure, of something like thirty-five per cent, admissions have gone up considerably since we put the tax on.
They are all making money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In Ontario I am sure the
increase in attendance would be much greater. Sometimes when I receive delegations now who predict ruin for themselves as a result of some taxation proposal, I take heart from my experience with those who made representations on behalf of the motion-picture industry. I have had other experiences of the same kind in the last two or three years.

How has the actual
revenue from this tax compared with what was anticipated?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is, I think, a little higher. I believe we anticipated $8,000,000 from the amusement tax and, if my memory is right, it amounts to about $8,500,000.
I suppose this is not considered a necessary of life by the wartime prices and trade board?

I hope the minister pays no
attention to the plea of the motion-picture people. Everyone of them is making money.

I am not surprised at the
remarks of the hon. member for New Westminster, because he said in the house the other day that he did not realize that there was a twenty per cent tax on motion-picture theatres.

The hon. member was not
sure of it himself.

I was very sure of it; I
said so at the time. I was glad a minute ago to hear the minister say he knew a number of small theatres were having a hard time. He will remember last year when this tax was before the committee I made an appeal that some of the small theatres should be given some concession. Of course he did not listen to it. In the meantime quite a number of small theatres in this country have gone out of business. I did not particularly object to the tax in the larger centres where there is a great deal of war work and great numbers of soldiers are stationed, but there are many small centres in Ontario where there is no war work, where no soldiers are stationed, and theatres in such places are under a great handicap. I do not know of any small theatre to-day in centres of this kind that is making any money. I suggest to the minister again that he should give some consideration to theatres in these small places, where there is only one in the town. It is the only place of recreation that a great many people have and, as he said himself, the difficulty has increased now that gasoline cannot be obtained for cars. The theatre is, therefore, left to depend entirely upon the population of the small town.
Is it only the night clubs that are to be included?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

What does the minister
mean by "similar places of entertainment" to a night club?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is a definition in the act, a very carefully drawn definition:
"Place of entertainment" means any place
1.	Where liquor, beer or wine is sold or provided, if facilities for dancing are provided for the patrons, or
2.	Where liquor, beer or wine is sold or provided, if entertainment by one or more paid performers is provided for the patrons, or
3.	Where facilities for dancing and entertainment by one or more paid performers is provided for the patrons, whether or not such place is enclosed or is in a building or other structure; but a place shall be deemed not to be a place of entertainment at any time when neither facilities for dancing nor entertainment as aforesaid by one or more paid performers are provided for the patrons.

I would not know that
of course, but I wanted to find out, because there seem to be so many others in the chamber who knew. I am surprised that I was almost alone.

I wish to bring to the
attention of the minister a letter which I received from a person I have not known but who is very much interested in the subject of five-cent cigars. He says:

That the duty of excise on spirits distilled in Canada be increased from nine dollars to eleven dollars per proof gallon, provided that duty paid spirits owned by any distiller at the close of business on the second day of March, one thousand nine hundred and forty-three shall be subject to the following additional duty of excise on every gallon of the strength of proof two dollars and so in proportion for any greater or less strength than the strength of proof and for any less quantity than a gallon.

I should like to make a few brief observations with regard to the regulations that have been passed under order in council P.C. 11374 of December 16, 1942. It took me a very long time to secure a copy of this order in council, though I tried to get it through the publicatons office. Finally I was fortunate enough to obtain a stencilled copy. At the present time it is rather hard for the average citizen to raise his elbow high enough to get any spirits, which of course are quite expensive now. I have no complaint to make in regard to the tax that has been placed upon such beverages. I congratulate the government upon having completely cancelled the fortified wines, which were quite an impossible beverage, but since spirits are now the privilege of the few, the wealthy, I wonder why there should be such restrictions on beer as are set out in this order.
Since we are now discussing alcohol, I think this is the proper time to say a few words about the beer problem, inasmuch as beer drinking may bring revenue to the government without injuring the health of the people. On this matter opinions may differ. But from the constitutional point of view I admit that all government policies should be first announced in the House of Commons, not over the radio. We are the ones who ought to know. We must be made acquainted in the first place with government policies, because members of parliament are the buffers for all legislation, and especially that which does not originate in this house.
I was greatly surprised to learn from a radio broadcast that certain restrictions were to be made, although I agreed with a few of them. I have no objection to the high tax on spirits.
1S68
Excise Act

I have no objection to the prohibition in respect of fortified wines. But I am aware there is a great deal of dissatisfaction among the people in connection with the way in which the beer problem has been dealt with. We hear the complaint that members of parliament were given no opportunity to express to the government the views of their constituents before action was taken. This is a matter which may be considered from several angles. When the government wants to know the feelings of the country at large with respect to any problem, it is very easy to ask members of parliament to give their opinions. If some acrimonious discussion is feared by the government, it is always easy to have the matter discussed among party members in caucus, or even to write to the members or to get in touch with them in some other way.
My first complaint-and I have several grievances-is that the matter was announced over the radio, and not in the House of Commons. Members of parliament had no opportunity to make any observations on the matter. One may complain about the evils of intemperance. I would not go so far as to say that a man who drinks beer or even one who drinks strong liquor is intemperate. It is not the fact of taking an occasional glas3 of beer or drop of whisky which makes a man a drunkard. There are some who hold the view that if a man holds a glass of beer, a cocktail, or some other liquor in his hand he is a drunkard. Hon. members will remember the story of the old gentleman of ninety-three years of age who was asked, while attending a dinner, the secret of his good health. He said, "I never take a drink, and I do not smoke." Next to that old gentleman sat another one a year older. The second old gentleman looked just as alert as the first one, and when asked the secret of his old age he said, "I take my bottle of whisky every day, and I smoke a lot of cigars." That is a true story, and it proves that opinions vary.
We have heard a good deal about the sovereignty and the rights of parliament. This parliament has not to swallow beer or whisky, or anything of that kind, but it has to swallow a policy made at the request of a minority. We heard last year that the majority shall rule. That is my opinion, provided a question is put clearly and in a straightforward manner. I have already stated the view that if the plebiscite had been held under different circumstances, and if the question with respect to conscription for overseas service had been put fairly to the Canadian people, in the words, "Are you for or against conscription for overseas?" the answer would have been entirely different. We must look to the future. But if
[Mr. Pouliot.)
we are to speak about the opinion of the majority, then the majority must not be fooled, and they should be asked the question, "Are you for or against the restrictions on beer?" That is the question which should be put to the Canadian people? If the majority of our fellow countrymen express themselves as being in favour of repealing the restrictions, then let the government repeal those restrictions. But if on the other hand the majority of the Canadian people are in favour of maintaining those restrictions, then I am sure the hon. member for Springfield and myself will not speak about beer any more in the house. We will take it for granted that the majority of the people in Canada are against it, and we will speak no more about it.
We know that the humble working man, the humble labourer who works hard all day in a munitions factory or on a farm wants to relax when he reaches home at night. What does he find? He finds it is impossible to buy any liquor at the store, because it has been drunk by those who receive pensions, or who live on the fat of land during the day, with the result that there is nothing left for the working man. He has no means to buy a flask of whisky costing S6 or $7. He has no means to buy gin-and, by the way, there are two kinds of gin he should not buy, because it will make him sick. He says, "Well, they are taxing my cigars. I am ready to pay that tax. They are taxing my beer-and not only do they tax it, but they restrict it. At least I can have a cigar when I want one. But they make me thirsty, and sometimes I like a glass of beer afterwards."
Then there is the question of quotas and the date from which the restriction has been imposed. The broadcast of the Prime Minister took place on December 16 last and the restrictions applied to the twelve month period ending October 31, 1942. The beer to be consumed was to be 10 per cent less for the next year, but the beer consumed between November 1 and December 16 was deducted from the quota. The liquor laws as administered by the liquor boards of the various provinces vary considerably, but I think they will meet on one ground. The quota in each province is supposed to be 10 per cent less than the consumption of the previous period.
Another matter must be considered. The number of men in the different camps have been increased, but the quota will be based on the consumption during the previous period. For instance, there may have been 5,000 men in a camp during the first period, and this number may be increased to eight, nine or ten thousand. The result will be that the restriction will be twice as severe as is intended

Excise Act
by the order in council. It will be still greater because a month and a half have been taken off the period.
In my humble opinion every civilian should be ready to make all the sacrifices that are necessary for the winning of the war, but why ask the Canadian people to make sacrifices that are not necessary? There is no need to make the people miserable. How does this restriction on beer help the war effort? It makes labour discontented; it makes the soldier discontented; it makes the civilian who is working during the day and cannot get his glass of beer discontented. I cannot conceive how a regulation like that will help the war effort.
Opinions differ. I have great respect for those who hold views contrary to my own. I do not approve excess in drinking, but I contend that the poor man should not be made to do without his glass of beer when the rich man is able to have a glass of imported Scotch whiskey or any other expensive beverage that he desires. What harm is there to the war effort to use malt and the other ingredients needed to manufacture beer? I cannot see any harm in this, provided that the regulations of the different provinces are applied, provided that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police constables do their work conscientiously, and provided that our temperance laws are well applied.
I cannot believe that our Canadian citizens were all bad up to December 16 and that a general purification took place on that day when there was to be less beer available. I do not think they were better citizens and more patriotic after that date. I do not want to be hypocritical. I have been a witness of the smuggling of bad liquor that took place during prohibition days when the Scott act was hardly applied and this country was being deluged with smuggled whiskey of a low quality. I should not like to see a repetition of those days, and I know the parents of grown boys and girls would not like to see them return.
If these restrictions are not modified the people will be greatly dissatisfied. I do not preach dissatisfaction, but I tell the government that from what I hear in the stores and on the streets everywhere, the people are dissatisfied. It is a bad thing not to keep up the morale of the people during war. They are ready to do anything the government asks them to do, but they feel they are entitled to a little relaxation. During one of my elections a friend, who believed in prohibition, was making some speeches for me. It was cold and raining and when he was driving
back, and his friend said to him, "Why don't you have a hot punch?" He said, "Oh, no, I never touch it; I would die first." His friend said, "You are not well; you have a bad cold; try it." They stopped, and they had a hot drink made up with a little ginger in it. The fellow took it, and the next morning he was cured of his cold. He said, "Well, I do not know if I am so sure about the success of prohibition when one has a cold." When you, Mr. Chairman, are hoarse or have a frog in your throat the best way to cure it is to take rum and honey. I have already tried it on some of my colleagues at election time. That liquor was just used as a cure and was very successful. Therefore, sir, we urge moderation. I hope that the government will understand that. I would bet that in his heart the Minister of Finance agrees with me, although I am not so sure he will say so. But he understands human problems. I do not ask him to give a definite answer now, but I should like him to think over the matter and discuss it again with his colleagues, and then I hope he will give a satisfactory answer before the budget discussion ends. I will ask him once more not to make the government unpleasant to the people, so that the war effort should not be affected by the restrictions on beer.

Mr. Chairman, I want to
endorse all that the previous speaker (Mr. Pouliot) has just said about beer. I can understand why he is reelected to this house time after time. It is because he always has the courage to rise in his place and say what he thinks. In my opinion he is a 21-jewel man. I would suggest to the government that if they are considering establishing a federal bureau of investigation here similar to the one in the United States, then the hon. member for Temiscouata is the man to put in charge of that bureau.
I have already spoken in this house on the deplorable and chaotic beer situation in Canada to-day, and in view of the support I have received of my views from all over the country I regret that I did not, when making that speech, ask for an adjournment of the house in order to open up a full discussion on this disgraceful and unnecessary beer situation. I say it is unnecessary, Mr. Chairman, because our elevators and granaries are bursting with grain and1 we have had our greatest snowfall this winter, some 8i feet here in Ottawa, to supply unlimited water, and these are two of the main ingredients used in the manufacture of beer. To strengthen my argument further for the immediate removal of the
Excise Act

beer restrictions, I wish, to read a letter that I have received from the general manager of a large coal company in Alberta, the Alexo Coal Company, Limited. It is as follows:
Alexo, P.O. Alta., March 24, 1943.
Mr. John Turner, M.P.,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Sir:
We have read with considerable interest and much appreciation the speech you have made in the house on the 18th instant, with reference to the deplorable situation which has developed as a result of the severe curtailment of beer supplies.
We would say that, as a result of the present restrictions with regard to beer, very considerable discontent and unrest is developing amongst the coal miners.	These men have been
accustomed to their glass of beer when coming off shift and as they are now called upon to work long hours, six days a week, under arduous conditions they greatly resent being deprived of their beer. In this camp, despite vigorous rationing of our beer quota, our monthly supply has been exhausted since the 20th of this month and for the balance of the month there will he no beer for the miners. We have a considerable number more men working here this year than last and as our monthly quota, as you probably know, is based on a percentage of last year's consumption, there is just not enough beer to go around.
We trust that in view of the great need for continuous and expanded output of coal from the mines, and which can only be secured by having contented miners, your efforts to induce the government to reconsider their present policy of restricted beer supplies may be crowned with success.
With best wishes and our appreciation of your efforts, we are,
Yours very truly,
Alexo Coal Company,
General Manager.
That letter, sir, might well have been read when the house postponed its regular schedule business to discuss the fuel shortage, because in reality it kills two birds with one stone.
In again pleading with the government to rescind, before it is too late, that part of order in council P.C. 11374 which was mentioned by the previous speaker, in so far as it affects beer, I will say here and now that if that is not done I can see nothing but trouble ahead. There will be delays, possible strikes, discontent and unrest, as is indicated in the letter I have just read from a coal company manager. These troubles will continue to develop and the result will be a complete setback in all branches of our war effort. Make no mistake about that.
Further, the transferring of large numbers of troops to other centres-I could give a good illustration of that if I wanted to-thereby again cutting down the supply of beer already

rationed on a 1941-1942 basis will cause a condition that was certainly not contemplated or heretofore expected in Canada.
Again let me say that the cut in beer does not apply equally to all provinces. It cannot, because no two provinces had the same beer regulations and control before this order in council wTas put into effect.
As evidence of the movement of population from one area to another, all we have to remember is that Manitoba and Saskatchewan are to lose seven seats in this house as a result of that movement. What is happening with respect to the unfairness of the beer supply? Let me give an instance. As reported at present, a person is allowed only twelve pints of beer a month in British Columbia. Other provinces receive much more. To me that is next door to total prohibition. If it is not, then I am Henry Kaiser the shipbuilder.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, as the Lenten season will soon be over and thousands of our good Canadian people have denied themselves of their personal privileges for the period of forty days, and also forty nights, and because immediately following that we face the intense heat period, the hot and dry summer months, I again urge upon the government to remove forthwith the restrictions from beer in order that the population will remain somewhere near normal and that all labourers and workers may give of their best efforts in the winning of this war.
I repeat what I said in my speech on the budget, and what our own Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and Mr. Churchill and members on all sides of this house have stated with just pride-our war effort is magnificent. That is our record for almost four years of war, is it not? Well, we did it on beer, did we not? Let us go on to the victorious end. Keep on playing the game you are winning at. That is a sound principle which is acknowledged the world over.

I had not planned to speak on this controversial question raised' by two hon. members this evening. Since, however, the government has received some criticism, I think something should be said in defence of the very important announcement made by the Prime Minister last December. While I have discussed this subject on a number of occasions I have never hoped that I would be able to get members like the hon. member for Springfield to approach it from the same point of view that I do, but I think a great many people will agree that we cannot hope to defeat the axis powers by increasing our consumption of intoxicating liquors at the

Excise Act
alarming rate that has prevailed during the last two years. Hon. members might be interested .in knowing something of the methods followed by one of our partners in the present conflict. I refer to Russia. In an article entitled1 "Religious Liberty in the Totalitarian States", written by Reverend James Barr, M.P., he says:
Notwithstanding Soviet Russia's departure from the absolute prohibition of vodka, she continues seriously to attack the drink problem. It is the rule of the league of communist youth (comosols) that they shall not drink, smoke, nor take drugs. Young people agitate against the drunken festivals in the villages. Posters everywhere declare that alcohol is the enemy of the state. The advertising of alcoholic liquors is absolutely forbidden, and even in shops where vodka is sold, an injunction is sometimes displayed, "Vodka is sold here, but you are advised not to buy." Radio talks are given, urging abstinence. In the cinemas special films appeal to workers not to drink. The central art commission has official instructions to revise theatre and cinema productions with a view to the inclusion of anti-alcohol propaganda.
That is the sort of approach we should have to this question. Instead of permitting manufacturers and distributors to spend large sums in encouraging young people to drink, we should be taking public funds to place before the people the scientific facts regarding the injurious effects of excessive use of alcoholic liquor. Instead of that, however, we have one of our dollar-a-year men, who has been holding down several responsible positions, the owner of the New World. For some time he was in the United States as vice-chairman of the British purchasing commission, with very responsible duties to attend to. He was placed in the position of deciding how our shipping would be used. When I discussed the question a year ago I pointed out that over fifty miles of box cars of beer had been shipped under the supervision of Mr. E. P. Taylor; and the financial statement which he has presented to his shareholders would indicate that his company had a very substantial share of this business. But the most recent estimates I have available indicate that it would take over three hundred miles of box cars to carry the beer which has gone from Canada to Egypt and the Middle East.
The Ottawa Journal of Friday, February 12, carried quite a long editorial replying to an article which appeared in the Christian Century, published in Chicago, written by the Rev. E. M. Howse, minister of Westminster United Church, Winnipeg. In this article, which had a very wide circulation in the United States, Dr. Howse wrote:
The Canadian people who have seen the stranded freight cars have learned with amazement that while these have been waiting, other freight cars loaded with liquor have been rushing by with blanket priorities to tie up shipping space for 18,000 miles around the seaway to Suez. The cars that wait come from Canada's vaunted plants of war production. The cars that go gaily by (hundreds of them) come from central Canadian breweries. . . . These breweries are directed by men of potent influence in the Canadian government.
The editorial comment says:
Now if Mr. Howse had been at pains about the truth, anxious not to smear his own land in another country, he could have learned easily that his "stranded" munitions on railway sidings have nothing to do with beer-have, in fact, little to do with ships. Learned that certain surpluses of Canadian war production are held in Canada under a definite Canadian and British military policy. Mr. Howse would not have been permitted to publish the reasons for that policy, but his personal awareness of them would at least have saved him from accusations desperately misleading.
I submit that if the statement made by Mr. Howse was misleading and not in accordance with the facts, action should be taken under the defence of Canada regulations, because the article has received wide publicity in the United States, and our neighbours across the line are curious to know why shipping space for such a large volume of beer can be found when great quantities of other materials, which apparently could be used to good advantage in other parts of the world, are left stranded. The editorial continues:
Asks Mr. Howse: Why not beer from England, from Africa, from the United States, from the breweries of Cairo? The obvious answer is that there are some 5,000,000 British, Canadian and American soldiers to be supplied with beer, and that with Canadian beer shipments but a fraction of their needs, all the other breweries are busy, too.
If there are 5,000,000 British, Canadian and American soldiers in the middle east, a great many people will want to ask some questions regarding the conduct of the middle east campaign. Canadians have a right to know why such a large, volume of beer is shipped across the Atlantic when the shipping situation is so critical. Granted that men who are in action in the desert have the right to refreshment; I think the decision as to how much they should have should not be made by one who is interested in the brewing business.
Mr. Taylor, like the hon. member for Springfield, is a very patriotic citizen. The order which was brought down on March 22 contains a letter which Mr. Taylor wrote to the Prime Minister following his broadcast. Mr. Taylor said:
Some fourteen years ago I was required to make a decision as to whether or not I would
1S72
Excise Act

become permanently engaged in the brewing business. At that time, of course, I had before me the spectacle of the ravages prohibition had caused in north America. I found that the industry in the province of Ontario had, to a large extent, fallen into the hands of undesirable people who had been attracted to it by the large profits which went with law evasion. I finally decided that the repeal of prohibition was inevitable, that I could do a constructive job in the industry in Ontario and help eliminate the undesirable elements. This has now for the most part been accomplished.
However, after I listened to your December 16 broadcast to the nation on the subject of temperance and a total war effort, and since pondering over the text, I am filled with forebodings and believe that the constructive progress of the last decade is in danger of being completely wiped out.
Before I give you my comments, I would like to make three points perfectly clear:
1.	Although I have a very substantial stake in the brewing industry, I would be quite prepared to make any sacrifice which could be shown to be a contribution to the successful prosecution of the war.
2.	The recent cuts you announced on production will make no difference to the profits of this company available for distribution to the shareholders. The effect on our business will simply mean that we will pay one million dollars less in excess profits taxes.
If the order is to result in this one firm paying one million dollars less in excess profits tax, I think the Prime Minister's announcement was in the best interest of the state, because it will inevitably mean a decrease in the consumption.
3.	The brewing industry is the greatest foe of intemperance and the abuse of liquor laws because we know that our whole future depends on the support of public opinion which we can only have if the nation is temperate.
Here is an idealistic man, a crusader in the real sense of the word, who a number of years ago went into this business to write a new chapter in Canadian history.
In the light of the above, I must respectfully tell you that I believe the whole tenor of your broadcast was unfortunate in so far as it suggested to the mass of the Canadian people that they were drinking too much and thus adversely affecting the efforts of the armed services and munition workers. I do feel that if you had addressed your remarks to the relatively few who are intemperate, your message would have done more good. In other nations the moderate use of alcoholic beverages-particularly beer- has been given credit for making an important contribution to the war effort.
It has been proved over and over again that restrictions on the production and sale of alcoholic beverages inevitably produces more intemperance and law evasion. The only cure is education, coupled with the strict supervision of the people engaged in the retail sale. This last, of course, is a matter for the local authorities.
I am very much afraid, Mr. Prime Minister, that the cure you have prescribed for the
IMr. Nicholson.]
nation is going to prove very much worse than the disease and that much of the progress towards temperance which we have made in the last decade, since we abandoned prohibition, will be lost as a result of your action.
In the matter of banning advertising for the period of the war, I must most respectfully suggest that you did not give the real reason in your broadcast. Was it not because you were being pestered by the prohibition element and were anxious to placate them? I cannot believe that you would be so unfair as to ban advertising of one legally produced article because it is in short supply and not ban advertising of other products such as sugar, gasoline, tea, coffee, etc. which are also rationed and in short supply. By your action in this regard you have in effect told the public that you consider that the brewers and distillers of this country are engaged in an undesirable business and therefore you are not going to accord them the same treatment which other commodities receive, and which they are accorded in all other English speaking democracies. I do hope you will reconsider this aspect of your pronouncement and amend it so that we may again become self-respecting members of society.
Your speech leaves me in an unfortunate quandry. One hesitates to take issue publicly with the Prime Minister in a time of war. At the same time I feel so completely that you

who through your manifold duties and great responsibilities have little time for first hand investigation-have been very badly advised. You will realize that I have responsibilities to my shareholders and the public and I cannot maintain my self-respect if, completely disagreeing as I do, I accept your analysis and treatment of the matter in silence. Will you give me the opportunity to discuss this matter with you at an early date. It would be my expectation that I could demonstrate to you that it would be in the national interest to make some statement which would correct certain implications of your speech and leave the door open in the future for some readjustment if time proves that the country's war effort and morale will suffer from the restriction now in force.
E. P. Taylor,
President.
The Prime Minister quite rightly pointed out that the decision was not his; that it was the considered policy of the cabinet, and1 that no useful purpose would be served by an interview. The fact that the president of one of the brewing companies wrote in that vein would indicate that the government policy as announced last December was generally in the right direction. I should like to see steps taken, in addition to prohibiting advertising, for an educational programme sponsored by the federal government with a view to placing the facts before our people, as I suggested earlier.
One more word about Mr. Taylor. In this morning's mail I received a letter-I presume a similar one went to all members of parliament-from the Anglo-Canadian publishers, publishers of this magazine which has its head office in Toronto, called1 the New World. In

Excise Act
Ontario for some time it lias been illegal to publish liquor advertisements in magazines or newspapers. Mr. Taylor apparently has ambitions in the newspaper field. This paper has its editorial and advertising office in Toronto, at 100 Adelaide street west but its printing is done in Montreal in order to evade the Ontario regulations. This magazine is found on thousands of newsstands across the country. This letter says:,
The official record of the battle of Egypt prepared for the British war office has been published exclusively in Canada by the publishers of New World Illustrated.
An initial printing of 100,000 copies has been made available to the public on bookstands throughout the country; but believing that leading public men in Canada would like to preserve a permanent record of this heroic battle I am sending you, under separate cover, this specially printed edition for your library, with my compliments.
Yours truly,
Anglo Canadian Publishers Limited.
1 object to a story as- important as that of the battle of Egypt being given exclusively by a publication which apparently has been placed on the market for the key purpose of keeping liquor advertisements before the public. If hon. members look through this magazine they will see very costly and attractive advertising which has been carried. I think wartime information or some other government agency should have made the story of the battle of Egypt available to other agencies across the country that surely have as much right to a scoop of this kind as the publishers of the New World.
Therefore I hope that the administration will not take too seriously the opinions expressed by the hon. member for Temiscouata or the hon. member for Springfield, but rather will carry out a policy to provide that less beer and other intoxicating liquors are consumed by the Canadian people as we make our contribution to the defeat of the forces of fascism the world over.
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? Is he in favour of beer by the glass for the working people?

I am not an authority on the subject. I have not used beer myself, and I hesitate to prescribe conduct for the hon. member or anyone else. I do not wish to force my views on other people, but I do say that it is in the interests of the people of this country to carry on an educational programme-
I am in favour of that.
-that will reduce the consumption of alcoholic beverages.
That does not answer my question. Is the hon. member in favour of beer by the glass for the working man? That is all I want to know.
I have not any opinion as to how beer should be sold, whether by the glass or by the bottle.
Supposing it is sold in any way, even in a keg?

I am anxious that the working people of Canada shall have the best possible homes and clothing and food and that they shall not have to read magazines that are printed in Quebec in order to evade the laws of Ontario, sold on Ontario newsstands by concerns that are primarily concerned about increasing the consumption of beer.
I still want an answer to my question. Is the hon. member in favour of beer sold by the glass, bottle or keg to the working people?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Such a question is for the hon. member to answer or not as he pleases.

The statement made by the hon. member for Springfield this evening, namely, that British Columbia has been discriminated against, is something which I believe the minister should answer. I am not saying what should be done, but the matter has aroused a great deal of adverse feeling in British Columbia, that one province has been singled out for a greater curtailment than other provinces. The people of British Columbia think they are just as temperate as the people of any other province. They are asking why this treatment should be meted out to them. If the statement is not correct, they are entitled to some information from the minister.
Another matter that is disturbing to the people of British Columbia is the statement made on good authority that some leak occurred in Ottawa, with the result that certain interests in British Columbia bought thousands of dollars' worth of liquor and spirits and beer which is now in the hands of these men who are selling it to the public at exorbitant prices. Such statements arouse a great deal of antagonism.

There has been no discrimination between the provinces. Each province is treated on exactly the same basis; that is, the amount of alcoholic beverages authorized for each province is in proportion to the amount that was used in that province during the year ended October 31, 1942. Each province gets its quota on that basis, so that there can be no discrimination in rationing alcoholic beverages in that way.
Excise Act

I fully agree with one point mentioned1 by the hon. member for Mackenzie; that is, in connection with the publication of the magazine New World. I remember that this magazine was supposed to have its head office in Toronto; that it was printed in Montreal because in Quebec there were no restrictions on liquor advertisements, and1 then it was sold in Toronto and other cities of Ontario, with all that liquor advertising. There are some manufacturers of liquor who have branches in the United States. They are able to publish very fine advertisements in United States papers and periodicals which are permitted entry into Canada. If we are to have prohibition; if there is to be no advertising in Canadian papers and! periodicals by manufacturers of liquor or by brewers, let us not have these United States publications come into our country carrying advertisements which are prohibited in our own papers. I find that unjust. I do not see why we should let those papers in, which are just as much an inducement to drink whiskey, wine or beer, when our own papers have not the same right to publish such advertisements. That is something I cannot understand. In all fairness either these advertisements should be permitted in our papers, or the entry of these United States papers should be prohibited. I submit that to the minister on the ground of fairness. I do not see why a manufacturer should not have the right to publish an advertisement1 for liquor in a Canadian periodical of any description when he has that right in the United States, and when advertisements published in the United States are permitted to come into this country. There is the same inducement to people to buy that liquor. I hope the minister will see to this. If he really wants to be drastic we will support him, provided there is no back-door; but if he is too drastic people will become discontented who are now willing to do all they can for the war effort, but who need a certain appreciation on the part of the government, even if they have to pay for it.

The question asked by the hon. member for Springfield of the hon. member for Mackenzie is usually supposed to be a poser that will stop anyone who advocates proper restrictions on the consumption of liquor. The question goes something like this: Would you take away the poor man's beer? I never hear any of these people asking: Are you in favour of the working man having champagne? I am not particularly concerned with taking away or letting the working man have his beer if he wants it. I have lived with 
working people all my life, and I have never yet seen a working man suffer from lack of beer or whisky or that kind of stuff. I have seen a working man suffer from lack of food, from lack of clothing, from lack of proper education, or from lack of a decent home in which to live. As a matter of fact a working man suffers, not because his beer is taken away but because he is a working man, because he has no access to the means of life except by selling his labour to somebody else. There is only one way in which to put the working man on a level with all the rest of the community, namely, by raising him from the position of a working man to the position of a citizen who has the -right of access to the good things that the community produces, because he is a citizen and because he renders a service to the country. I am in favour of the poor man having everything he should have or, if you like, everything the rich man can have because he is rich; but I am not in favour of giving him "his beer" just because beer is a cheap drink. I should like to see him asking for the things all the "best people" have, and then I am satisfied that he will get beer along with all other good things.

According to the schedule given it would appear that there is no change in the present rate as compared with the rate which has been in existence heretofore. Would the minister indicate just what is happening?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is a change in the item, not in the rates, and a very important change it is. Since 1890 the various items covering spirits have contained a proviso that no reduction or allowance shall be made in the measurement of quantity for duty purposes of imported spirits below the strength of fifteen per cent under proof. This proviso is now deleted, and duty will henceforth be assessed on the actual strength of proof. Item 156a, covering rum, has been amalgamated with 156, the item covering spirituous liquors generally. The tariff rates attached to both items have been the same for a number of years.	Prior to
March 2 the customs import duty on whisky or other spirits was levied on the assumed strength of fifteen per cent under proof, Sikes hydrometer.	A case of twelve computed
quarts of whisky contains two imperial gallons, or 1-70 proof gallons, when duty is computed on the basis of fifteen per cent under proof. Imported whisky is about twenty-five per cent under proof, and the quantity on which customs duty is payable under the amended item 156 would be 1-50 proof gallons, a reduction of -20 of a gallon per case. Under the wartime alcoholic beverages order, 1942, which is P.C. 11374, dated December 16, 1942, no person shall sell, offer to sell, supply or deliver any spirits of any alcoholic strength greater than seventy per centum proof spirits, which is thirty per centum under proof.
When it is illegal to sell spirits of a strength greater than thirty per cent under proof, the same prohibition would apply to the importation of spirits and it therefore becomes highly artificial to impose a duty on the water content. To continue the provision that a duty shall be levied as if it were only fifteen per cent under proof when it must be thirty per cent under proof, is getting one's law far away from one's facts. Therefore, the law is being amended so that the duty will be levied on the actual strength of the liquor. The reason for the fifteen per cent provision seems to have been to assist in ascertaining the actual strength; there was considerable trouble in ascertaining what the actual proof strength of the liquor was. The debates at the time have been examined, and there does not seem to have been much discussion on this curious provision. The Minister of Finance took the ground that we would call it all fifteen per cent under proof. I presume the duty was pretty low at the time, and therefore it did not make much difference. The officials just were not
going to the trouble to find out what the real strength was; they were going to call it fifteen per cent under proof.
The minister refers to fifteen per cent under proof. As a matter of personal curiosity I should like to know what is meant by that phraseology in the act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The definition of proof spirits is found in the interpretation section of the customs tariff.
Perhaps hon. members would like to know what it really means.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is going into the matter pretty deeply. In the interpretation section of the customs tariff it is given as follows:
"proof", "proof spirit" or "proof spirits", means any spirit having the strength of proof by Sikes' hydrometer, that is, spirit which at the temperature of fifty-one degrees fahrenheit weighs exactly twelve-thirteenths of the weight of an equal measure of distilled water at the same temperature.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The present item is being widened in scope to provide for advances and developments that have taken place in the production and use of nickel and its alloys since the item was established in the tariff a number of years ago. The former item read:
Customs tariff-355. Nickel in ingots or blocks, n.o.p.; nickel bars and rods, not including bars or rods depolarized or otherwise processed for use as anodes; and nickel in strips, sheets or plates.
The amended wording reads:
Customs tariff-355. Nickel, and alloys containing sixty per cent by weight or more of nickel, n.o.p., viz.: ingots, blocks and shot; shapes or sections, billets, bars and rods, rolled, extruded, or drawn (not including nickel processed for use as anodes); strip, sheet and plate (polished or not); seamless tube.
Substantially the whole of the nickel imported into Canada either in the pure form or as alloys is produced from Canadian ores. There is no rolling mill in Canada capable
Customs Tariff

of producing nickel rolled shapes. In view of the extremely limited consumption of the Canadian market it is unlikely that any such mill will be established in the foreseeable future.
The object of the former and revised item covering nickel in various forms is to enable the duty free reimportation of nickel that has been processed in the United States, thereby encouraging the production of primary nickel and at the same time placing the Canadian manufacturer on an equal basis with the United States manufacturer.
It is to be noted that the former item and the new item both provide for nickel in ingots or blocks, but "shot" has been added to the classification, because this is one form in which pure nickel is produced, and is in fact more generally used than ingots or blocks.
It is also to be noted that the former item provides for nickel bars and rods, while the new item provides for shapes or sections, billets, bars and rods, rolled, extruded or drawn. The forms covered by the new items have been somewhat extended to include all modern rolling mill products of the material in question.
Both the former and new item provide for strip, sheet and plate.
Seamless tube is included in the proposed item. No seamless tube of high nickel alloys has ever been produced in Canada.
The new item specifies that nickel and alloys must contain 60 per cent by weight or more of nickel. This qualification is inserted to facilitate administration. The scope of the new item as far as nickel content is concerned is in fact broader than the scope of the former item.
Certain combinations of nickel with other metals, such as "K" monel, "KR" monel, 'Z" nickel and a nickel alloy known as 'Inconel", will now be definitely covered by ;he new item. These forms were formerly, in most instances, dutiable under tariff item 711 at the United States trade agreement rate of twenty per cent.
It is estimated that annual imports in norma] times of nickel forms, not admissible under tariff item 355, amounted in value to about 8100,000. In the calendar year 1942, imports under tariff item 355 amounted to 881,316 pounds, valued at SS04.224.

The convention is out of existence now. Under the former item importation was restricted to films entitled to entry under the convention for facilitating the international circulation of films of an educational character. Under the new item films, etcetera, are admitted duty free when they are certified by a government or by a ' recognized representative authority of the government of the country of production as being of an international educational character.
The convention for facilitating the international circulation of films of an international character was signed at Geneva on October 11, 1933. That is what is out of existence. There is no certifying authority.

That is the administrative
reason?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Then the government does not fully accept the word of another government as to the educational value of a film?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is subject to such regulation as the Minister of National Revenue may prescribe. He may accept the certificate of a recognized representative authority of the country of production. If he gives a certificate that the films are of an international educational character the minister may let them in. But he may prescribe regulations.
Are they examined before they are distributed in this country?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Department of National Revenue inspects them to see whether they are educational before it lets them in.
Do the provincial motion-picture censorship boards not inspect them before they are allowed to be distributed in the provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That has to do with their showing in the province. That is a different matter.
The federal government might let a film in, but a provincial government might keep it out?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Might not let it be shown in that province.
Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is another atnendment. The motion is:
That schedule A to the customs tariff, as amended by resolution No. 1 of March 2, 1943, be further amended by striking thereout tariff item 704 and by inserting in lieu thereof the following item, enumerations and rates of duty.
This is a long item, but it covers a very small matter.

May I interrupt the minister? This item may or may not be of great importance. It is very difficult to assess the importance to be attached to any of these items. But the minister in a previous resolution in connection with the budget was good enough at an earlier date to bring down the amendment in the matter affecting the one-cent postage. I should have liked if the minister had given us a little more opportunity at least to read over the amendment before we are asked to pass it. I cannot at the moment see anything that would be specially
Customs Tariff

difficult in this instance; on the other hand I think we ought to have an opportunity of going over it and seeing what it is about.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I agree. If these were not very small matters we would not try to do it this way. But unless I am making some mistake about these it is very important.
I will not support any amendment that I have no chance to read.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Then we better move that the committee rise. I will move this amendment and put it on the record and let the hon. member for Davenport read it. It has to do with letting some bequests from abroad in free of duty. It will not upset the economy very much. It reads:
704. Apparel, wearing and other personal and household effects, not merchandise, of British subjects dying abroad, but domiciled in Canada; books, pictures, family plate or furniture, personal effects and heirlooms left by bequest to any resident of Canada, or acquired by any resident of Canada as a result of the death of any person resident abroad, or as a gift in anticipation of the death of any such person; all such goods or articles when given as a free gift by anyone resident abroad to a resident of Canada; the minister to be the sole judge as to whether any goods or any article imported is to be classified as entitled to the benefit of this item or not: British preferential tariff, free; intermediate tariff, free; general tariff, free.
The former item has been widened in scope by the addition of all the words after the word "bequest" in the fifth line thereof. During the past few years several cases have occurred in which gifts of personal effects, including pictures, books and furniture, have been given by a member of a family residing abroad to relatives in Canada. This has become more frequent of late, owing to people moving into smaller quarters or giving up winter homes in the southern states. While free entry can be permitted in the case of bequests, this does not apply to gifts made in contemplation of death or under the circumstances outlined above.
During the calendar year 1942 imports under item 704 were valued at S123,085, of which $110,000 worth came from the United States, and $11,000 worth from the United Kingdom. There were a few imports from Jamaica, Newfoundland, Australia and New Zealand. It is estimated that the widening of the scope of this item will result in about ten per cent increase in imports.
Progress reported.
